n: By lot. Manuscript 2 reads bogurl; (printed benachala) so the Vulgate sortito. (Kennicott) --- Hebrew, "when you shall make the land fall," which usually implies by lot: yet the partition was not made thus, (chap. xlviii. 1.) nor at all, (Calmet) otherwise the prophet might mention how the lots would have fallen to Dan, in the north, &c. (Haydock) --- The Jews either could not comply, or did not take this to be a command. If they had returned all together, they might probably have put it in execution. But many of them preferred staying where they had gotten a settlement, and the rest only returned in small parties, some not before the reign of Alexander [the Great]. Those who arrived first, occupied as much as possible their ancient limits, 1 Esdras iii. 1., and 2 Esdras viii., and xi. (Calmet) --- Thousand: reeds, or cubits. (Challoner) --- Many prefer the latter, which is specified [in] ver. 2., (Haydock) as it agrees with the dimensions of the temple, chap. xlii. 16. If reeds or toises were meant, the city would be disproportionate with the rest of the divisions: 50,000 would make 25 leagues, of 2,500 paces each; and if each tribe had as much, the country must have comprised 325 leagues, whereas from Emath to Cadesbarne (chap. xlvii. 17.) there at[are?] not above 150. (Calmet) --- To form an idea of the proposed partition, we must suppose the country reached from a little north of Emesa, on the Orontes, to Cadesbarne south, and from the Mediterranean to Damascus, or a little farther east, and beyond the sources of Jazer. 1. Dan, 2. Aser, 3. Nephthali, 4. Manasses, 5. Ephraim, 6. Ruben, and 7. Juda, had about equal portions with that designed for 8. the temple, the Levites, and prince, whose southern limits reached almost to Accaron and the Dead Sea. 9. Benjamin, 10. Simeon, 11. Issachar, 12. Zabulon, and 13. Gad, had each about half the quantity of the others, though the tribes occupied the whole extent from east to west, their lots being marked out by parallel lines. Between Juda and Benjamin, a square of 500 cubits was assigned for the temple; another square of 4,500, or 18,000 in circuit, lay round the former for the city of the Levites: round this were suburbs 250 cubits broad, walled about, and having three gates on each side. Next them dwelt their lay servants, in a space 5,000 cubits broad, and 25,000 long, from east to west. A plot of ground on the north and south, sufficient to complete this square was to support them with provisions. On the east side of the Jordan, and on the west of this square for the priests and their servants, two portions almost of equal dimensions with it, were appropriated to the prince. His lot was 25,000 cubits long, and 12,500 broad, chap. xlviii. 21. See Calmet's plan. (Haydock) --- About. It could not be alienated to private men, or for any other purpose. (Worthington)
Suburbs. Hebrew also, "vacant spaces."
Measure, from the centre of the temple; so that the dimensions given must be doubled, (chap. xlviii. 10.) as also ver. 5.
Place. There the priests shall dwell.
Chambers for the Levites on duty. Septuagint read, "towns." But only one seems to be specified, 18,000 cubits in circumference.
According. Hebrew, "along or (Calmet) over-against the oblation of the holy portion." (Protestants) --- Israel, destined to serve the priests. (Haydock)

Border. Two equal lots, one on the east and the other on the west, were assigned the prince, each 20,000 cubits broad, and 12,500 long, chap. xlviii. 21. (Calmet) --- He dwelt near the priests, for their protection; as the people were on both sides of him, that he might sustain no injury. (Worthington)
Rob. Instead of their right, (1 Kings viii. 11.) the source of continual vexations, a certain revenue is specified, ver. 13.
Confines: encroach not. (Calmet) --- Hebrew and Septuagint, "take away your oppressions;" (Haydock) Chaldean, "scandals." (Calmet)

The ephi and the bate. These measures were of equal capacity; but the bate served for liquids, and the ephi for dry things, (Challoner) ver. 13, 14. (Worthington) --- Ezechiel specifies the measures, that the people might not use those of Babylon, after their return.
Sicles. It would be shorter to say, "sixty sicles make a mna."
Take, for the prince's revenue. He had the sixtieth part of corn and of oil; or rather (Calmet) he had an exact tithe of the latter, ver. 14. (Chaldean) (Menochius)

One ram. He shall receive the tithe of sheep, &c., and take one out of two hundred, on condition that he furnish victims, ver. 17. (Calmet) --- The obligation was mutual. St. Jerome explains it of the high priest and people. (Worthington)

Holocaust. This was given before perhaps gratis, 2 Paralipomenon xxxi. 3. Solomon and Ezechias shewed great magnificence. After the captivity the people laid on the third of a sicle per head, as this order was not observed, 2 Esdras x. 32.

Take, or order the priests to do this annually, to prepare for the Passover, ver. 21. Moses mentions nothing of this, and it does not appear to have been put in execution. (Calmet) --- Yet it might be the first year after the dedication of the temple. The prophet does not say it was to be done every year. (Haydock)
Seventh, or so many days before the solemn feast. Septuagint, "on the first of the seventh month," the feast of trumpets, Numbers xxix. 1. (Calmet)
Sacrifice. Hebrew mincha, flour. Protestants, "meat offering." (Haydock)
Day: the feast of tabernacles, to be observed like the Pasch, Numbers xxix. 12. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

But if we wish to compare spiritual things with spiritual and, following certain interpreters, to climb to higher things — they assert that the present things are a figure of things to come, and that all that is said pertains to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all, and to the Church of the firstborn —, it will not indeed be difficult to say what has been said by others, but we fear that the prudent reader may by no means accept an exposition of this kind; hence all things are to be referred both to the present time and to the Church, which now labors in the world and hastens to go to heavenly things: so that out of the whole world some are chosen as a possession of God to possess the holy place, and others, who have advanced to greater things, to hold the Holy of Holies; in the ministries too the order of priests and Levites is different: some of them daily offer sacrifice to God by their prayers and virtues, others are in a second and lesser rank, so as to minister to these, and through those who have climbed to the summits of the virtues; and last of all there is a leader or prince who has such power that he receives a possession over against one tribe and by the merit of one balances the merits of very many, and first, while he lives in the world, possesses the breadth from sea to sea, then from the west, or from the sea, as far as the east, so that, leaving the present things behind, he may hasten to the things to come, and may have his own fixed possession, and the prince may by no means desire what belongs to others, and each tribe may hold its own part: which can properly be referred to bishops and presbyters, to whom it is said that they should no more lay waste and ravage the people of God, nor possess the land of Israel as an inheritance, but that each should have his own possession, the one appointed to his rank. Now the twenty-five thousand they refer to the senses, which are set down four times; and the ten thousand to perfect knowledge, so that in the one only the plain history is held, while in the other there is discussion also of θεολογίᾳ [theology] and of the heavenly powers, because ten is a perfect number. This too must be considered: that the priests, who are set in the higher rank, possess twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth; but the rank of the Levites, that is, the lower one, has indeed the same number in length, that is, twenty-five thousand, but its breadth is bounded by the number five: hence too they hold only twenty chambers — the number in which the gifts for Esau are offered —; but the prince, who is truly a prince among the people and deserves to receive the name of leader, receives a possession of the sanctuary on this side and on that, namely from all who are subject to him of their own will, and he is a dweller in the city, and makes the salvation of many his own reward. In the first temple, which is called the sanctuary, five hundred reeds are described on each side, and again fifty cubits by which the whole possession of the priests is separated; but in the second sanctuary, where the Holy of Holies is, the breadth of the temple and its space are not described, but the number is uncertain: and this we find also in the possession of the prince, who has a possession among the people of Israel without any number, since the progress of all overflows to the prince: and the salvation of the disciples is the reward of the teachers.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when you begin to divide the land as a possession, set apart firstfruits to the Lord, a sanctified portion of the land, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth; it shall be sanctified in all its border round about. And of this there shall be a sanctified portion five hundred by five hundred, four-square round about, and fifty cubits for its suburbs all around. And from this measure you shall measure a length of twenty-five thousand and a breadth of ten thousand, and in it shall be the temple (or the sanctification) and the Holy of Holies. The sanctified portion of the land shall be for the priests, the ministers of the sanctuary, who approach to the ministry of the Lord; and it shall be a place for them for houses and for a sanctuary of holiness: twenty-five thousand of length and ten thousand of breadth. But the Levites who minister to the house, they shall possess twenty chambers (for which the Seventy translated: they shall hold a city to dwell in). And you shall give the possession of the city five thousand in breadth and twenty-five thousand in length, according to the separation of the sanctuary, to the whole house of Israel. To the prince also, on this side and on that, by the separation (or the firstfruits) of the sanctuary in the possession of the city, over against the face of the separation of the sanctuary and over against the face of the possession of the city, from the side of the sea to the sea and from the side of the east to the east, and of length along each part, from the western border to the eastern border, of the land: it shall be his possession in Israel, and the princes shall no more ravage (or lay waste) my people; and they shall give the land to the house of Israel according to their tribes. After the ceremonies of the priests, and their worship and their food — what they ought to take and what to avoid —, he now gives a description of the holy land; and before he divides the whole land among the tribes, he commands that out of all the tribes a place be chosen which should have twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth — and since 'of cubits' or 'of feet' or 'of ells' is not set down, we are given to understand that it signifies 'the reed', which was in the man's hand and had a measure of six cubits and a sixth part of one cubit, that is, a παλαιστήν [palm, a handbreadth]: let the diligent reader reckon how many reeds make a thousand paces and how many thousands there were in length and breadth —; after this description he again commanded that, from the sanctified land which was chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, that is, of twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in breadth, another land within, of five hundred reeds round about, that is, of two thousand, be chosen for building the sanctuary, that is, the temple of the Lord. And lest perhaps other buildings should be joined to the building of the temple, he commanded that for fifty cubits round about the land be empty 'for suburbs', or, as Symmachus, Theodotion and the Seventy translated, 'for a boundary' and 'a separation' and 'a space'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

When this description is finished, another measure, of a sanctification to be set apart, is prescribed afresh: that after the former measure another land be measured, of twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in breadth, in which there is by no means the temple, that is, the holy place, but the Holy of Holies.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And in it let the priests dwell who approach to the ministry of the Lord; and let them dwell there at the time when they discharge the priestly office: and let this possession be, as we have said, of twenty-five thousand reeds in length and ten thousand in breadth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Further, the Levites, who serve the priests and have ministries of their own, will receive a place for building twenty 'chambers' — according to Aquila; 'exedras' according to Symmachus; 'cells' according to Theodotion; or, as the Seventy translated, 'a city', by which we understand that a certain separate place for the dwelling of the Levites is called by the name of a city —, a place which is to have five thousand reeds in breadth and twenty-five thousand in length. All these things, that is, the sanctuary and the second sanctuary, and the Holy of Holies, and the dwellings of the priests and the houses of the Levites who minister to the priests, are called places separated and consecrated for ministry and for sanctification for the house of Israel.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After the fourfold description of the holy land a fifth division is set down: that the prince or leader of the people should receive on this side and on that, that is, on either side of the sanctuary, for his possession, and should dwell in the city, and that his possession should face the place set apart for the temple and the face of the city, and should be from the side of the sea, that is, from the west, as far as the other side of the sea, having the breadth which the prophet describes below in the description of the individual tribes. Then follows: But in length along each part — which the individual tribes receive — from the western border — that is, of the sea — as far as the eastern border — where this ends we learn in the description of the tribes —; and this will be the possession of the leader or prince in the land of Israel. These things have been said for the present so that the plain account of the history may be known.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: Let it suffice you, princes in Israel; leave off iniquity and plunder, and do judgment and righteousness: separate your borders from my people, says the Lord God. For 'plunder' the Seventy translated 'misery'; for 'borders', 'oppression'. And the sense is: 'Since you have received your portion, O princes — as Scripture says: To the prince also on this side and on that, in the separation of the sanctuary, in the possession of the city (understand: you shall give) —, and your power is so great that your possession has received the portion of one tribe: therefore I command and admonish you that it suffice to have committed iniquity and plunder up to now, while you invade and snatch away what belongs to others; and — since it is written: Put away evil and do good, and conversely: Do judgment and righteousness, judging for the orphan and justifying the widow —: Separate your borders from my people, namely so that you do not move the boundaries, and because the very neighborhood harms the humbler man, who cannot bear the haughtiness of one greater and more powerful. Let this be said for the present to the people of that time; but the command can also be fitted to our own princes — who after the manner of Pharaoh and the Egyptians oppress the children of Israel through their power, and do not remember that it is written: Have they made you leader? Do not be lifted up, but be among them as one of them —, and also that which the Lord says in the Gospel κατὰ [according to] Luke: But if that servant says in his heart: My master delays to come; and begins to beat his men-servants and maid-servants, and to eat and drink and be drunk: the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect and at an hour that he does not know, and will divide him, and will put his portion with the unbelievers; his disciples too he instructs with these precepts in the Gospel according to Matthew: You know that the princes of the nations lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise power over them; it shall not be so among you, but whoever wishes to be great among you shall become your minister, and whoever wishes to be first, let him be the servant of all. Just as the Son of man came not to be ministered to, but to minister, and to give his life as a redemption for many: there are many passages, if I wished to unroll them from the sacred Scriptures, where the pride of the greater is restrained and all are called to the humility of the Lord, who says: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart.
Commentary on Ezekiel

A just balance and a just 'oephi' and a just batus you shall have; the 'oephi' and the batus shall be equal and of one measure, so that the batus holds a tenth part, and the 'oephi' a tenth part: according to the measure of the 'corus' shall be their equal balancing. And the shekel has twenty obols; moreover, twenty shekels and twenty-five shekels and fifteen shekels make a mina. (LXX: "A just balance and a just measure and a just choenix you shall have for measure, and likewise there shall be one choenix for receiving: the tenth part of the gomer the choenix, and the tenth part of the gomer the 'oephi'; in relation to the gomer it shall be equal, and for weight twenty obols: twenty shekels, five and twenty shekels and fifteen shekels shall be your mina.") This passage, according to the Seventy, does not hang together and cannot be understood at all, since they changed not only the numbers of the measures but also the names: for in place of 'oephi' they translated 'measure', a general name for a specific one, and in place of 'batus' 'choenix'; in place of the Hebrew 'omer' too, which in Greek is called 'corus', they translated 'gomor', and again in place of 'batus' 'choenix'. Let us therefore speak according to the Hebrew and the letter, and let us explain more plainly what seems right to us in each particular. The 'balance', which in Hebrew is called 'mozene', is understood of the things that are weighed; but the 'epha', which in the Greek language is corruptly called 'oephi', pertains to the measure of various crops, for example wheat, barley, legumes; moreover the 'batus', which in Hebrew is called 'bath', is the same measure as the 'oephi', and only in liquid kinds, wine and oil and other things of this sort; the 'corus' holds thirty modii, and in both measures, that is, of dry things as well as of liquids, it holds the first place; the tenth part of the 'corus', in things that are measured by the modius, is called 'epha' — that is, three modii — and the tenth part of the 'corus' in liquid kinds is called 'batus' or 'badus': so that the 'epha' and the 'batus' are of the same measure; moreover the 'siclus' [shekel], which in Greek is called 'stater', has twenty obols; but the 'mina', which in Greek is called 'mna', has sixty shekels, which make one thousand two hundred obols; but what he says: Twenty shekels and twenty-five shekels and fifteen shekels make a mina, ought not to disturb the reader: for the difficulty is placed in the numbers for this reason, to make the hearer's mind attentive — whence also many things are spoken in parables and riddles, as: He who has ears to hear, let him hear; and all prophecy contains the truth in obscurity, so that the disciples may hear within, while the ignoble crowd placed outside may not know what is being said —. The divine Scripture therefore commanded that weights be just — saying: There shall not be in your purse a large measure and a smaller. A true and just balance you shall have, and a true and just measure you shall have; and in Proverbs it is said: A large balance and a smaller, both are abominable in the sight of God —, which indeed is to be observed by us not only in commerce and in the use of daily life, but righteousness must be guarded in all things — as Scripture says: By your words you shall make a balance and a weight —, so that, in words and in deed and in thoughts, we may do all things by weight and reason. That the obol, that is, the twentieth part of the 'siclus' or stater, is the smallest little portion, we read in another place: To the one who is faithful, the whole world of riches; but to the one who is unfaithful, not even an obol — as if he had said in other words: 'The unfaithful man possesses nothing in the world, but lacks even the smallest portion', of which it is said in another word in the Gospel: He shall not come out from there until he pays the last quadrans, that is, even the very last and smallest coin —; we read of ten minas handed over to individual servants for trading, and in another parable of talents divided among servants, and of the debtor of five hundred denarii, and of fifty, and of the laborers of the vineyard who each receive a denarius, and of the widow woman who lost a drachma and scarcely found it again by lighting a lamp: what sense all these things have, this is not the time to discuss.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And these are the firstfruits which you shall take: the sixth part of an 'oephi' from a 'corus' of grain, and the sixth part of an 'oephi' from a 'corus' of barley. The measure of oil also, a batus of oil, is the tenth part of a 'corus'; and ten bati make a 'corus', because ten bati fill a 'corus'. (LXX: "And these are the firstfruits which you shall set apart: the sixth part of a measure from a gomor of wheat and the sixth part of an 'oephi' from a 'corus' of barley. And the ordinance of the oil: a cotyle — that is, a cyathus — of oil from ten cotylae, because ten cotylae are a gomor.") Here too, the names of the measures having been changed, everything in the edition of the Seventy is confused, so that what is said cannot be understood: for they who above had said 'measure' for 'oephi', and 'choenix' for 'batus', and 'gomor' for 'corus', 'weight' for 'siclus', here too say 'measure' for 'oephi', for 'corus' now 'gomer', now 'corus' itself, and in the measure of oil 'cotyle', that is, 'cyathus', for 'batus'. Let us therefore speak first according to the letter. Δεκάτας — that is, the tenth part — of all crops the people owed by the law to the Levitical tribe; again, from these very tithes the rank of the Levites — that is, of the lower ministers — gave tithes to the priests, and this is what is called δεύτερον δεκάτη [the second tithe] — there were also other tithes, which each one of the people of Israel set apart in his own granaries, so that he might eat them when he went to the temple in the city of Jerusalem, and in the vestibule of the temple they would invite both priests and Levites to banquets; and there were also other tithes, which they stored up for the poor, which in the Greek language are called πτωχοδεκάται [poor-tithes] —; but the firstfruits which they offered from their crops were not defined by a specific number but left to the discretion of those offering, and we have received a tradition of the Hebrews, not commanded by the law but grown into custom by the discretion of the teachers: he who gave the most gave the fortieth part to the priests, he who gave the least the sixtieth; between the fortieth and the sixtieth it was permitted to offer whatever they wished; what therefore was left doubtful in the Pentateuch is here specifically defined on account of the avarice of the priests, so that they may not exact more from the people in the bringing of firstfruits, that is: that they offer the sixtieth part of the things that grow from the earth — for if the 'corus', which in Hebrew is called 'omer' and by the Seventy is called 'gomer', holds thirty modii in dry kinds as well as in liquids, and the 'epha' and the 'batus' too, according to what we said above, are the tenth part of the 'corus', and it is commanded that the sixth part both of the 'oephi' and of the 'batus' be given to the priests in offering the firstfruits, which out of three modii makes half a modius, it is clearly reckoned that the priests ought to receive the sixtieth part as firstfruits —. Let it suffice for the meantime to have perceived and heard these things according to the letter and according to the Hebrew truth. Now let us return to the spiritual understanding, in which it must first be asked how it is said: 'Honor the Lord from your righteous labors, and give him the firstfruits of the fruits of your righteousness, so that your storerooms may be filled with grain, and your winepresses may overflow with wine, so that, after you have offered the firstfruits of your labors and virtues and have said: Behold, now I have brought you the firstfruits of the fruits of the earth, which you gave me, O Lord, you may deserve to hear: Blessed are you in the city and blessed in the field; blessed the children of your womb and the produce of your land, and the fruit of your beasts and so on, and you may possess — according to the Apostle — every blessing of spiritual things in the heavenly places in Christ, while you hold that whatever you have is not of your own virtue but of the mercy of him who gave the crops'. And if indeed we have so much knowledge of the Scriptures that we lay open all the mystical things and teach men, that is, the rational animal, we give the firstfruits of our grain; but if, after ἀναγωγὴν [anagogy, the higher sense], we follow only the pure history, which can nourish the simple — according to what is written: Men and beasts you will save, O Lord —, we give the firstfruits of our barley — which barley: Isaac also served in the land of the foreigners, and it rose for him a hundredfold —. He who gives the firstfruits of barley can say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing: in a place of pasture, there he has placed me, beside the waters of refreshment he has brought me up, but he who feeds rational living creatures with grain turns the sentence and says: You have prepared a table in my sight against those who trouble me, and after he has offered the firstfruits of oil and wine he joins on and says: You have anointed my head with oil, and your cup that inebriates, how splendid it is: with that oil which is prepared, most pure, without dregs, for the lamp of the Lord — and whoever has prepared it: His face is gladdened with oil, with the oil of exultation with which Christ was anointed above his fellows, and, made an olive tree, he will sing with the prophet: But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God —, and with that wine which overflows from the true vine in the winepresses of the Savior — as the Lord says: I am the vine, you the branches, my Father the vinedresser —; of these winepresses we read three psalms, Psalm 8, Psalm 80 (81) and Psalm 83 (84), all of which refer to the mysteries of the Church. And indeed in the old law the firstfruits were without measure and number: For God did not give the Spirit by measure; but in the second building of the temple, which the prophecy of Ezekiel contains, there is a fixed measure, that is, the number sixty: by which the world is filled up, and it is said to us: With whatever measure you have measured, it will be measured back to you.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And as in the preceding we read that the sixtieth part of the things that are weighed and that are subject to measure ought to be offered to the prince, so now the two-hundredth part of the living creatures is commanded to be offered, and the whole people is subject to the precept of this law and of this command: that it offer to the leader or prince, because, of course, through him holocausts and sacrifices and libations are offered for the people at each solemnity, and the house of God is expiated; from which it is to be noticed that, as the people is debtor to offer firstfruits to the prince, so the prince is debtor to the people to offer victims for it; and him, according to tropology, we can understand as none other than God the Savior. He receives a ram out of two hundred living creatures — or, as the Hebrew word shows more significantly, βόσκημα [a grazing beast], which can refer to all living creatures and not properly to a ram —, and he receives the animal or ram which has been nourished in irrigated places, namely those of the holy Scriptures, and can say: The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing: into a place of pasture, there he has placed me, beside the waters of refreshment he has brought me up; these were the irrigated places, nay rather these the channels, to which Jacob too led his flocks, so that in them they might drink and conceive and, according to the color of the rods, bring forth offspring for the Lord. In place of 'sacrifice', that is, θυσίᾳ, Aquila and Symmachus translate 'gift', which in the Hebrew is called 'manaa', and it properly pertains not to a victim but to the things which are offered in sacrifice from fine flour and parched grain and oil; but the 'holocaust' is what is offered whole to God and consumed by the sacred fire; the 'peace offerings', when we are reconciled to God: and on our behalf the Apostle says: We pray on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God, and in another place: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. But this prince, to whom the firstfruits of living creatures are offered, is himself the king, as is shown also in the title of the cross in Hebrew and Greek and Latin letters — and when the Jews strove to have the triumphal title taken down, the throng of the Gentiles, in Pilate, answered: What I have written, I have written —. Upon the prince, he says, shall be: finely is the priestly dignity reminded to what office it is subject, so that it may know that it ought to offer for the people the sacrifice and the libations which are offered from wine at all the solemnities: namely at the calends, that is, the new moons, as well as at the sabbaths, when, with darkness covering all things, there is the beginning of the moon's light, in the rest of the sabbaths: so that he may make, namely, for sin, to make expiation for the house of Israel, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth: for this is the house of the living God and the house of Israel, which needs the expiation of its sins.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And one ram from a flock of two hundred, from those which they nourish in Israel, for a sacrifice and for a holocaust and for peace offerings, to make expiation for them, says the Lord God. All the people of the land shall be bound to these firstfruits for the prince of Israel; and upon the prince shall be the holocausts and the sacrifice and the libations, at the solemnities and at the calends and at the sabbaths: at all the solemnities of the house of Israel: he shall make the sacrifice for sin and the holocaust and the peace offerings, to make expiation for the house of Israel. Above he said what portion of the things that are weighed, and of the measures too, both of dry kinds and of liquids, ought to be offered to the prince; now he keeps the same order of firstfruits in living creatures, and commands Israel to offer one out of a flock of two hundred rams: Which Israel nourishes, for a sacrifice and for a holocaust and for peace offerings, to make expiation for the people of Israel, says the Lord God. What we translated: From those which Israel nourishes, is written in the Hebrew 'memmasce', which Aquila and Symmachus translate ἀπὸ τῶν ὑδάτων, the Seventy and Theodotion ἀπὸ τῶν ποτιστηρίων: of which the one means from irrigated places, the other from channels or pools, so that, evidently, the firstfruits of the prince are nourished nowhere else but in irrigated places.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: In the first month, on the first of the month, you shall take a calf from the herd without blemish, and you shall expiate the sanctuary. And the priest shall take of the blood of what will be for sin, and shall put it on the doorposts of the house and on the four corners of the ledge of the altar and on the doorposts of the gate of the inner court. And thus you shall do on the seventh of the month for each one who was ignorant and was deceived by error, and you shall make expiation for the house. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, you shall have the Passover, a solemnity; for seven days unleavened bread shall be eaten. And the prince shall make on that day, for himself and for all the people of the land, a calf for sin; and in the solemnity of seven days he shall make as a holocaust to the Lord seven calves and seven rams without blemish daily for seven days, and for sin a he-goat of the goats daily; and the sacrifice he shall make of an 'oephi' for each calf and an 'oephi' for each ram, and a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi'. In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the solemnity he shall do as has been said above, for seven days, both for sin and for the holocaust, and in sacrifice and in oil. (I have set down the whole chapter so that, divided into its single parts, it should not confuse the reader's mind; and first we must speak about the variety of the translation; where we translated: On the four corners of the ledge of the altar, the Seventy translated: And upon the four corners of the temple and upon the altar; and where we said: For each one who was ignorant and was deceived by error, they put: For the ignorant and the little one; also in the place where we said: And the sacrifice he shall make of an 'oephi' for each calf, an 'oephi', and an 'oephi' for each ram, and a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi', their edition has: And the sacrifice and a cooking for the calf and a cooking for the ram you shall give, and a 'hin' of oil for the cooking; in the last little verse too, where we said: In sacrifice and in oil, they said: As in the manaa, as in the oil.) In the first, he says, month and on the first day of the month — no doubt he means Nisan —, and: You shall take a calf from the herd, not one which has been nourished at home but one in the herd, that is, from the flock and number of many; on the seventh day of the same month too: these two solemnities, that is, the first day of the first month and the seventh of the same, are not found in the Mosaic law; but the fourteenth day of the month, on which the Passover is celebrated, Moses too commanded to be observed: when we eat unleavened bread for seven days; but the fourth solemnity, of which he says: In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day of the month, at the solemnity and so on, seems to me to signify the Scenopegia [the feast of Tabernacles], which he has set down here without a name. Let us run back, then, to the particulars, and briefly discuss what seems right to us. That there are spiritual solemnities too the Apostle teaches: Let no one therefore judge you in food or in drink or in solemnities or of the new moon or of sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come; and if God says through Isaiah: Your new moons and your sabbaths and the great day I do not accept: the fast and the holidays and your new moons and solemnities my soul hates, it is manifest that he who hates the solemnities of the Jews loves his own, namely the sabbath which is left for the people of God: That we may see the things that have been given to us by God: and may speak not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual: for in the present age, which is set in the evil one, we cannot see good days, but in the new, of which days the Holy Spirit sings in the Mosaic song: Remember the days of antiquity, understand the years of the generation of generations, of which the holy man also spoke in the psalm: In the night I meditated in my heart, and again: And I had the eternal years in mind and I meditated; let him who has not accepted this understanding answer how he can expound what Isaiah prophesies about the future and new age: There shall be month from month and sabbath from sabbath, and all flesh shall come to worship the Lord, when the true worshipers will by no means worship on Mount Gerizim nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth, when there will be a new heaven and a new earth and: The whole creation shall be freed from the servitude of corruption into the liberty of the children of God and the sun will receive seven times as much light and the moon will be compared to the sun: We have come, indeed, to Mount 'Sion', which means 'watchtower', and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to thousands of angels' solemnities, of which solemnity another prophet also speaks: What will you do in the days of assembly and in the days of the solemnity of the Lord? this is what is also said elsewhere: Celebrate, Judah, your festivals, pay your vows.
Commentary on Ezekiel

If then we have learned spiritual solemnities, we shall consequently be taught spiritual victims too: a calf is taken from the herd — or a bull, as Symmachus translated —, free and pressed by no yoke, that is, by the burden of sins, and without blemish: Who did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth, a young calf putting forth horns and hoofs: so that in him the sanctuary may be cleansed and expiated.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the priest, he says, shall take of its blood which will be for the sin of all, who in other words is called a lamb in Exodus, and in the Gospel, as John the Baptist says: Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world; and the blood itself is precious, in which we are redeemed in the passion of the Lord Savior, by whose flesh we are fed and with whose blood we are given drink, by which are touched the four corners of the ledge of the 'altar' — for which Theodotion put the Hebrew word itself, 'azara' [ledge, court], or of the 'temple', as the Seventy translated —, so that the house and the altar may be sanctified — for all the elements of the world are sanctified by this blood — so that, when someone has been expiated and cleansed, he may enter the gate of the inner court and be able to know the secrets of the Lord, and consequently come to the seventh day of the first month and attain rest and offer sacrifice to the Lord: both for ignorance — of which David speaks: The sins of my youth and of my ignorance remember not —, and for the little one — who, when he has come to the measure of the perfect man, destroys the things that belong to a little one and speaks confidently: When I was a little one, I spoke as a little one, I thought as a little one —, or for him who was deceived by error and sinned not so much by will as by the supposition of good.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when the two solemnities of the first month have been completed, that is, of the first day and of its seventh, he comes to the fourteenth day of the month, on which is the solemnity of the Passover, of which it is written: For our Passover has been sacrificed, Christ; then we eat unleavened bread for seven days in rest and security of all things, when, destroying the leaven of malice and wickedness, we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, while our prince offers all these things for us: and first 'for himself' — for he took up a human body and for sin destroyed sin, he who grieves for us and bears our infirmities —, then 'for his house' — which is written in the Seventy but is not found in the Hebrew — that is, for the Church, and for all the people of the land, namely the whole human race: He is the Savior, indeed, of all men and especially of the faithful; and he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not only for us, but for the whole world.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when the calf has been offered for all the people of the land, on the seven remaining days of the Lord's passion seven calves and seven rams without blemish are offered daily, so that they may be burned up as a holocaust and by the Lord's fire: and the seven calves and seven rams are those who are conformed to the Lord's passion, so that they may imitate the true calf and the true ram, and by the blood of the martyrs through seven days the sins of the whole world may be cleansed; a he-goat of the goats too is offered for sin daily, namely for seven days.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And it must be noted more carefully that in the sacrifice an 'oephi' for each calf and an 'oephi' for each ram and a 'hin' of oil are offered, which are commanded by the law, but in the offering of the he-goat neither an 'oephi' nor, as the Seventy translated, a 'cooking' is set down — they who for 'oephi' translated πέμμα, that is, 'cooking' —; but the 'hin', which is a fixed measure of oil, of which we have already spoken before, is taken up in the sacrifice of the calf and of the ram, so that we may receive the fuel of everlasting light, and rest from labor, and healing from weariness after the appeasement of sins.
Commentary on Ezekiel

In the seventh month too, on the fifteenth day of the month, that is, of the Scenopegia, the same order of oblation and sacrifices is to be kept: Both for sin and for the holocaust and in sacrifice and in oil, so that, darkness having been put to flight and the light of the oil having risen, we may attain the festival of the Lord, and may have brighter solemnities, in which all our sins are forgiven us.

n: Prince. After the captivity, although the race of David continued in Salathiel, Zorobabel, &c., yet they had not the state of kings. Hence Christians, R. David and other Jews, understand this of the Messias and the rites of his Church, with a literal allusion to the old law. (Worthington) --- Without, not proceeding into the court of the priests, chap. xliv. 2.
Six. Moses only prescribed two lambs for every day, Numbers xxviii. 9.

Sacrifice. See chap. xlv. 24. Flour and oil accompanied the victim. When lambs were presented, this was left to the prince's devotion (ver. 7, 11.; Calmet) only. If he gave three or four ephies of flour, he must give as many hins of oil. (Haydock)
Calf. Moses orders two, and seven lambs, Numbers xxviii. 11. (Calmet) --- The rams. Hebrew, "a ram. They shall," &c. (Haydock)

It, perhaps to avoid confusion, (Menochius) and turning the back on the temple, (Calmet) or to exercise their obedience. As many might enter by one gate as by another, and thus the concourse would not be diminished. (Haydock)

Out. The prince went in and out by the same gate, (ver. 8.) and might order that on the east to be opened when he had to offer a voluntary sacrifice. In other respects he was like a simple Israelite, and was to attend the temple and use the same gates as the rest. Before, the kings had a gate on the west leading to their palace. But this was no longer to subsist, and the palace was to be far removed, chap. xlviii. 21.
Solemnities. Hebrew, "on feasts and on days of meeting." (Calmet) --- Sacrifice: mincha, ver. 7., and chap. xlv. 24. (Haydock)
Morning. That for the evening had the same ceremonies, Leviticus vi. 9.
By. Cata seems to be taken (Calmet) from the Greek kata, "according to," or by, ver. 15. (Haydock)

Sons. If any portion of his land was made over to them, it still remained in the family; but if any other had a present of it, the land must revert to the royal family, agreeably to the law, Leviticus xxv. 10. (Calmet) --- This insinuates that works done by the true children of God, in the state of grace, merit an eternal reward, while moral good works performed in the state of sin, can only have a temporal one. (Worthington)

Gate, on the north, chap. xliv. 4. --- West. At this corner was the kitchen for victims, which could only be eaten in the inner court. If they had been brought into that without, the people would have become unclean; as it is equally wrong to touch holy or impure things when they are forbidden, chap. xliv. 19. There were four other kitchens for the people who might choose to eat their peace-offerings, ver. 24. (Calmet)

Little. Hebrew, "courts joined;" (Protestants) or marginal note, "made with chimneys," (Haydock) or "smoked," as no chimneys were used. Septuagint, "little courts," as they have read differently. (Calmet) --- Vulgate unites both meanings. (Haydock)
Kitchens. Septuagint, "porticoes," or rather (Calmet) "boiling places;" (Protestants) and ver. 24. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

Let these things be set down for the sake of clarity; now, the Lord granting, let us unfold the spiritual sense. During the six days on which we work in the world, the eastern gate of the inner court is shut to us; but after we have come to the seventh day, that is, to the sabbath day on which there is eternal rest, or to the day of the kalends, when after blind night and dreadful darkness there is the beginning of light, the eastern gate is opened to us; and if any of us, through the merits of the virtues, has attained the name and dignity of a leader, he will enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate from outside, that is, through the labors of this world, and through the gate of the Church, which is still set within earthly bounds, not into the inner court — for this is what is written in the present passage — but to the threshold of the inner gate: and he will stand in it; but if the prince in the present scripture does not enter the inner court, but stands on its threshold, no one doubts that we now see in part and know in part, and do not yet contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. Then, while the prince stands on the threshold of the gate of the inner court, the other priests, to whom this office has been delegated — whom we can understand as the angelic powers —, will make for him the holocaust and peace offerings — for we need the mercy of God, and every creature, in comparison with the Creator, is unclean and must be purged by the divine fire, by which the lips of the prophet Isaiah too were purged —, so that, after he has received peace through the sacrifice, then, standing on the threshold, he may worship the omnipotence of God and confess himself unworthy of entering the inner court, and at once go out; but after he who is first has gone out, that very gate of the inner court will not be shut until the evening of this age, but will be open, so that the people of the land too may be at the entrance and worship toward him: by no means at every time, but when they have rested from sins and, the darkness of faith having been put to flight, have received the light of knowledge.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And meanwhile, before we discuss what these things signify, the very words of Scripture must be laid open παραφραστικῶς [by way of paraphrase]. The gate, he says, of the inner court on six days — of which it is written: Six days you shall labor and do all your works — shall be shut, and not just any gate, but the one that faces toward the east, whence the sun of righteousness rises; further, on the sabbath day, that is, the seventh, on which there is rest, it will be opened every week, and again, when thirty days are completed, when there is the end of one month and the beginning of another, on the new moon, namely the day of the kalends, it will be opened, so that the privilege the seventh day has in the week, the beginning of the month may have as its privilege too.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But why the gate of the inner court that faces toward the east is opened on the seventh day and on the day of the kalends, the following discourse will show: And the prince shall enter, he says, by the way of the gate from outside — namely of the outer court —, and shall stand on the threshold of the gate — of the inner court, which faces the east —, and he shall not enter the inner court, but, while he stands, other priests are to make for him the 'holocaust' — which Symmachus translated 'offering' —, and the peace offerings — or those which pertain to salvation —, so that, after the prince's victim has been burned up by the sacred fire and the leader has been reconciled to God, he may then worship upon the threshold of the gate of the inner court on which he has stood, and go out. What then? After the prince's going out will the gate be shut at once? By no means, but it will be open until evening, so that after the prince: All the people of the land may worship before the entrance of that gate: and they are to worship on the sabbaths and on the kalends, when the gate is opened.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And since he had said above: The priests shall make his holocaust and his peace offerings, and had not indicated the number of the holocaust, he now adds: And this holocaust the prince shall offer to the Lord on the sabbath day — he will offer it, however, not by himself, but through the priests, of whom it is written: And the priests shall make his holocaust and his peace offerings —: six, he says, lambs without blemish and a ram without blemish, so that the sacrifice of the ram is the measure of an 'oephi' — which in Hebrew is called 'epha' —, while for the six lambs the sacrifice is what the hand of the one who offers was able to offer, and for each 'oephi' there will be the measure of oil that is called 'hin'; but the kalends, that is, the day of the new moons, had this privilege beyond the sabbath day, that: A calf from the herd (or a bull) without blemish be sacrificed, while the rest, that is, the six lambs without blemish and the ram without blemish and their sacrifices, will keep the rite of the sabbath, only in such a way that, just as with the ram an 'oephi' of sacrifice is offered, that is, of fine flour, and a 'hin' of oil, so it is offered with the calf too.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And this very holocaust, which the prince offers through the priests on the sabbath day, is bounded by the number of six lambs without blemish — namely after the six days on which we work in the world — and a ram without blemish, which is the prince of the flock, so that for each ram an 'oephi' is offered in sacrifice, that is, the tenth part of a 'corus'; but in the sacrifice of the six lambs no fixed measure is laid down, but as much as the hand of the one who offers shall give, that is, according to the quality and measure of his works; and he will offer a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi' — that is, the oil which the five virgins prepared for themselves —, to anoint the fine flour or mix it, so that every offering to God may be full of the light of truth, and the face of the one who offers may be made glad with oil; but on the day of the kalends, that is, the thirtieth day, when the firstborn and the Levites are numbered according to the law apart from all Israel, of whom we spoke above, a calf from the herd without blemish is offered — about which we discoursed more fully in the previous chapter — and six lambs and a ram without blemish, and the rest that are offered on the sabbaths, so that we may attain eternal rest and may deserve to hear: Well done, good servant, because you have been faithful in a few things, I will set you over many: enter into the rest of your Lord, and may be able not only to come to the gate of the inner court but also to enter its innermost parts, and to possess in deed that saying: Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: The gate of the inner court that faces toward the east shall be shut on the six days on which work is done; but on the sabbath day it shall be opened, and on the day of the kalends also it shall be opened, and the prince shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate from outside, and shall stand on the threshold of the gate, and the priests shall make his holocaust and his peace offerings, and he shall worship upon the threshold of the gate, and shall go out; but the gate shall not be shut until evening. And the people of the land shall worship at the entrance of that gate on the sabbaths and kalends before the Lord. And this holocaust the prince shall offer to the Lord on the sabbath day: six lambs without blemish and a ram without blemish, and a sacrifice of an 'oephi' for the ram, but for the lambs a sacrifice such as his hand shall give, and a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi'; but on the day of the kalends: a calf from the herd without blemish, and six lambs and a ram shall be without blemish, and an 'oephi' for the calf, an 'oephi' also for the ram he shall make as a sacrifice, but for the lambs as his hand shall find, and a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi'. Where we have translated 'oephi', which is the tenth part of a 'corus', the Seventy translated πέμμα, which in our language means 'cooking'; and where we said 'sacrifice', they set down the Hebrew word itself, 'manaa', which Aquila translated 'gift' or 'sacrifice', Theodotion 'sacrifice'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when the prince enters, let him enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate, and let him go out by the same way. And when the people of the land enter in the sight of the Lord on the solemn feasts, he who enters by the gate of the north to worship, let him go out by the way of the southern gate; and he who enters by the way of the southern gate, let him go out by the way of the gate of the north: he shall not return by the way of the gate by which he entered, but shall go out opposite it. But the prince in their midst shall enter with those who enter and shall go out with those who go out. And on market days and on solemn feasts the sacrifice shall be an 'oephi' for the calf and an 'oephi' for the ram, but for the lambs the sacrifice shall be as his hand shall find, and a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi'. That prince, of whom it was said above: And the prince shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate from outside, is both to enter by the same way and to go out by the same way: for he is of free will and has power to lay down his life and to take it up again, and, as much in coming to us as in ascending to the heavenly places, he uses the same freedom of his majesty.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Then too, he does not seek market days or solemn feasts, nor does he observe any difference of days, because every time is a festival as well; but the people enter and go out only on market days and on solemn feasts, and not by the same way, but by one way and then another: for it is written: And when the people of the land enter in the sight of the Lord on the solemn feasts, he who enters by the gate of the north to worship, let him go out by the way of the southern gate; and he who enters by the way of the southern gate, let him go out by the way of the gate of the north: he shall not return by the way of the gate by which he entered, but shall go out opposite it — which is commanded not only to those who go out of Sodom, and to whom it is said: Do not look back, nor only to those who put their hand to the plow, that they not look back at the things that are behind their back, but those too who are set in the house of the Lord are commanded not to look behind their backs and return to the weak and beggarly elements, and, having begun in the spirit, be finished in the flesh, but to advance from spiritual things also to greater ones and to say with the Apostle: Forgetting the things past, and stretching myself out to the things before, so that they may by no means know in part and prophesy in part, but come to the perfect: yet according to that perfection which human nature can contain, so that we may understand that saying of the Gospel: And you, when you have done all things, say: We are unprofitable servants; what we ought to do, we have done; whence the Apostle too, in the same epistle, speaks of two perfections: for as one perfect he writes: Not that I have already received, and that I am already perfect; but I pursue, if I may lay hold of that in which I also have been laid hold of by Christ, and at once he speaks as one perfect: But one thing: forgetting the things behind, stretching myself out to the things that are before, I pursue according to the purpose toward the prize of the upward calling. As many therefore as are perfect, we are of this mind — for how can the statement stand, that he who had said: Not that I have already received or that I am already perfect, should dare to say: As many therefore as are perfect, we are of this mind? —, from which it is plain that every human being and the whole creation, although it has come to perfection, nevertheless needs the mercy of God and possesses full perfection from grace, not from merit —. And so the people of the land are commanded that, if they enter by the gate of the north to worship, they go out by the way of the southern gate. Who is this people to whom this is commanded? Surely that of the Gentiles: so that he who, leaving the gate of the north — from which: Evils blaze up upon the earth —, has entered the temple, should not go out except by the way of the southern gate, to the gate of light, to the gate of warmth, to the gate at which the bridegroom lies at noon; and indeed it is said in the same Song of Songs: Arise, north wind, and come, south wind. But he who enters by the way of the southern gate also goes out by the way of the gate of the north. Which people is that? Clearly that of the Jews, which, leaving the way of the gate of light, goes to the gate of the north — of which it is said: The north wind is a most harsh wind; for Jeremiah's pot too is kindled from the face of the north —. Let us say it another way too: he enters by the gate of the north who lets go of sins, and he goes out by the southern gate who follows the virtues; and conversely, if a righteous man has fallen into sins, he enters indeed by the southern gate, but goes out by the way of the gate of the north.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the prince, he says, in their midst will be, namely in the midst of those entering and going out, according to what is written: In the midst among you stands one whom you do not know, and the Apostle: Or do you not know that Christ is in you? — but if it is said to those who do not know that Christ stands in their midst, how much more to those who know; but when Christ has stood among those who know, then the body will become dead because of sin and the spirit living because of righteousness! —; and the prince enters with those who enter, and goes out with those who go out, standing by as witness of both, of virtue and of sin.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Therefore on market days and on solemn feasts — namely of the sabbaths and kalends and of every festival, of which we have spoken earlier — both with the calf and with the ram a single 'oephi' will be offered in sacrifice; but with the lambs there will be no fixed number, nor is the choice left to the will, but one will use his strength and the good of his conscience, so as to offer as much as he can, not as much as he wishes; and over all, a 'hin' of oil for each 'oephi', so that the fine flour may be anointed and the lamp lit in the sight of the Lord, and those who use it may be able to say: But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But when the prince makes a spontaneous holocaust or voluntary peace offerings to the Lord, the gate that faces toward the east shall be opened for him, and he shall make his holocaust and his peace offerings as is usually done on the sabbath day, and he shall go out, and the gate shall be shut after he has gone out. And a yearling lamb without blemish he shall make as a holocaust daily to the Lord; morning by morning he shall make it. And a sacrifice (or manaa) he shall make with it morning by morning, a sixth part of an 'oephi' (or of a measure), and of oil a third part of a 'hin', to be mixed (or according to Symmachus sprinkled) with the fine flour; a sacrifice (or manaa) to the Lord, lawful, continual and perpetual. You shall make the lamb and the sacrifice and the oil morning by morning, an everlasting holocaust. Where we read 'without blemish' and in the Hebrew is written 'thamim', Aquila translates 'perfect'; and where the Seventy have 'manaa', Theodotion translated 'sacrifice', Aquila and Symmachus 'gift'; and for what we said, 'spontaneous', the Seventy rendered ὁμολογίαν, that is, 'confession'; and for 'prince', 'leader', for this is what 'basi' means. Moreover, the discourse is still about the prince — of whom Isaiah speaks: Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a prince and instructor among the nations, and Ezekiel: And I the Lord will be their God, and David a prince in their midst —. When therefore this prince makes a spontaneous — and says: The voluntary (or spontaneous) things of my mouth make well pleasing, O Lord —: and a 'spontaneous' holocaust, so that he offers the whole to God, and 'voluntary' peace offerings — which is not found in the earlier passages, for it is written: And the priests shall make his holocaust and his peace offerings, and about the spontaneous and voluntary ones, of which it now speaks, there is complete silence —, so that he does it not by necessity but by will; after the holocaust let him offer peace offerings, and be reconciled to God — whence virginity too is greater than marriage, because it is neither exacted nor rendered, but offered —; for 'peace offerings', which in Hebrew are called 'selamim', the Seventy translate 'saving offerings': so that the very reconciliation of the peace offerings may be the salvation of the one who offers. When therefore the prince has done this: The gate will be opened for him (or, according to the Seventy, he will open the gate for himself) that faces toward the east — that gate, namely, of which it is written: This is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter by it, and whence the sun of righteousness rises —. And he shall make, he says, his holocaust and his peace offerings — of which we have just spoken —; and 'he shall make': as being a spontaneous sacrifice, and not other priests 'shall make' it for him: namely as is usually done on the sabbath day; therefore at every time the holocaust and peace offering that is offered voluntarily has the gate of the Lord unbarred, and it does not observe the sabbath, but all days are reckoned to it as rest. Then, after he has offered the holocaust and peace offerings, at once: He goes out, and the door is shut after him (or he shuts the door), so that the prince's privilege may be kept for him and his sacrifices not be mingled with the people.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And since he had said in general: A spontaneous holocaust or voluntary peace offerings to the Lord, and had not added bull or calf, ram or sheep, and a he-goat for sin, he teaches what this holocaust is: A yearling lamb, he says, without blemish he shall make as a holocaust; and not on fixed days, but: daily; nor at any other hour, but: morning by morning he shall make it: namely each 'morning', when, the sun having risen, there is the beginning of light — of which 'morning' David speaks in a psalm: In the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will stand before you, and will see, and in another place: In the evening weeping will linger, and in the morning gladness, and again: O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the morning. But who this lamb without blemish, or perfect, and yearling is, Isaiah teaches more fully, saying: As a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer, without voice and not opening his mouth, and Jeremiah: But I, like an innocent lamb led to the slaughter, did not know, and John the evangelist: Behold the lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world; this is the lamb that is sacrificed in Egypt and with whose blood the doorposts of faith are armed, and the destroyer is shut out; and a yearling, because: He proclaimed the acceptable year of the Lord, the day of retribution. Nor let the reader wonder if the same one is both prince and priest and calf and ram and lamb, since in the holy Scriptures, according to the variety of circumstances, we read of him as Lord and God and man and prophet and rod and flower and root and prince and judge and righteous king and righteousness, apostle and bishop, arm, servant, ointment, shepherd, son and child, only-begotten and firstborn, door, way, angel, arrow and wisdom, and many other things, for all of which, if I wished to cite the testimonies, they would need a book of their own —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And so in the holocaust of this lamb, without blemish and a yearling, which is always offered in the morning: the prince himself shall make a sacrifice (or 'manaa', and fine flour or gift) morning by morning, a sixth part of an 'oephi', of fine flour being understood — and a sixth part of an 'oephi' is half a modius; for if an 'oephi' is the tenth part of a 'corus', that is, three modii, no one doubts that the sixth part of an 'oephi' makes half a modius —. Of the oil also, a third part of the measure 'hin' is offered, to be mixed (or sprinkled) with the fine flour; a sacrifice to the Lord, lawful, continual and perpetual, which is interrupted on no day but at every time, when the sun has risen, is always offered, so that what is set at the end of this chapter may be fulfilled: He shall make the lamb for a sacrifice, and the oil, morning by morning, an everlasting holocaust.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God: If the prince (or leader) gives a gift to any of his sons, his inheritance shall belong to his sons; they shall possess it by inheritance. But if he gives a legacy from his inheritance to one of his servants, it shall be his until the year of remission (for which Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, deror), but it shall return to the prince; but his inheritance shall belong to his sons. And the prince shall not take from the inheritance of the people by violence and from their possession, but from his own possession he shall give an inheritance to his sons, so that my people be not scattered, each one from his possession. Thus far the discourse about the prince; now precepts are given about his heirs, or rather about gifts, inheritance and legacies: to whom he ought to give, and whose the possession is, whether for a time or everlasting. 'If', he says, 'he gives either a gift or an inheritance to his sons, they will possess it, because it is owed to them by right of succession, and the possession cannot pass from one to another; but if he gives it to one of his servants under the name of a legacy, he will hold the possession only so long as until either the seventh year, of remission, which is called 'deror', or the jubilee, that is, the fiftieth, arrives, when every purchase and gift will return to its former owners: so that the servant has the use for a time, and the sons of the prince the ownership of the possession'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But what follows: And the prince shall not take from the inheritance of the people by violence (or, as the Seventy translated, so as to oppress them, or, as Aquila and Symmachus, afflict them and sadden them), but from his own possession he shall give an inheritance to his sons, censures not only the priests and princes of that time but also those of ours, who grow richer through the dignity of the priesthood and, beyond what is owed them by the Lord's ordinance, take from the poor by violence, or despoil the rich under the name of honor, so that even to their own sons, to whom the paternal inheritance is owed, they ought to leave nothing except what was left to them by their parents; therefore the priest who is richer than when he came to the priesthood ought to give whatever more he has, not to his sons, but to the poor and to the holy brothers and to those of the household of faith, who surpass the merits of his children, so that he may render to his Lord the things that are the Lord's — who speaks in the Gospel: Whatever you have done to one of these, you have done to me; for he himself, in the poor, is received in hospitality, visited in prison, clothed when naked, drinks when thirsty, is filled when hungry —: So that my people be not scattered from its possession: for if the prince has license either to take or to seize or to hold under the guise of honor what is not his and to leave it to his children, the people that had been gathered in the name of God will be scattered into parts and torn apart, or, according to the law, the inheritance of one may gradually pass to another and the cord of division perish, through which, as it happened, the inheritance came to each one; therefore he scatters the people of God and takes from it the everlasting possession of faith who leaves to his sons and brothers and kinsmen the goods of others, whether by plunder or by flattery or by blandishments or under the pretext of religion.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he brought me in by the entrance that was at the side (or behind the back) of the gate into the chambers of the sanctuary for the priests (or exedras, and cells) that faced toward the north, and behold, there was a place sloping toward the west (or toward the sea, and, as the Seventy translated, separated); and he said to me: This is the place where the priests will cook for trespass and for sin (or for ignorance and for sin), where they will cook the sacrifice (or manaa, and gift), so that they do not carry it out into the outer court and the people be sanctified. And he brought me out into the outer court and led me around through the four corners of the court, and behold, there was a little court in a corner of the court, a little court in each corner of the court. In the four corners of the court little courts were laid out, of forty cubits in length and thirty in breadth: the four were of one measure. And a wall round about encircled the four little courts, and kitchens were built beneath the porticoes all around (or beside the couches, which Aquila translated στιβάδας [pallets], Symmachus περιφράγματα [enclosures], while Theodotion set down the Hebrew word itself, turoth). And he said, he says, to me: This is the house of the kitchens, in which the ministers of the house cook the victims of the people (or victim, for this is what zeba means in Hebrew). The man who held a reed in his hand and a mason's cord with which to measure the building: 'He brought me in', he says, 'by the entrance that was at the side of the gate (or behind the back of the gate) — and he did not state which gate, the eastern, the southern or that of another quarter, but left it uncertain —, so that I went to the place of the sanctuary and into the chambers, or rooms, of the priests, which faced toward the north and toward the sea': namely toward the northern quarter and toward the west, Holy Scripture having this custom, that by reason of the position of the land of Judah it always calls the west the sea — and it must be considered that the place of the priests where for trespass (or for ignorance) and for sin the sacrifices are cooked, lest they be carried out raw into the outer court, is set toward the north and the west, whence the coldest wind arises and where the light of the sun goes down; from which it is shown that whatever pertains to food is either for error or for sin: but if a sacrifice is offered even for ignorance, how much more for the consciousness of trespass!: whence Job too offered a victim every day in the morning for his sons, fearing lest they had transgressed through ignorance —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But what follows: 'So that they do not carry it out into the outer court and the people be sanctified, the people who had not been prepared for sanctification', signifies this: that we should not readily give holy things to the unsanctified; that we should not, according to the Gospel, cast pearls before swine nor give what is holy to dogs — indeed Moses wishes the people to be sanctified for three days from all uncleanness and from the embrace of wives, so that they may approach Mount Sinai and, sanctified, receive holy things. But if those about to approach to hear and receive the words of God are commanded to be sanctified from their wives, it is manifest that that apostolic saying too is contained in the law: Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by consent for a time, that you may be free for prayer; and that by consent one must abstain from wives, that we may be free for prayer —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

After this it is written: And he brought me out into the outer court and led me around through the four corners of the court, and behold, there was a little court in a corner of the court, a little court in each corner of the court; in the four little courts of the corner, little courts laid out; that man whom he often mentions brought him out of the place of the priests which sloped toward the north, or which was separated, where the priests cook for trespass and for sin or ignorance; and he brought him out into the outer court: from which we understand that the court from which he went out was the inner one, and that there are many courts in the holy Scriptures — of which we read: You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God, and in John: And other sheep I have, which are not 'of this court'; and them too I must bring: and they will hear my voice, and there will be one 'court' and one shepherd — for this is what the Greek αὐλή means, which Latin simplicity translated as 'fold' —: for when he says 'of this court', he shows that there is another as well, which is pointed out either in the throng of the nations, as distinct from Israel, or in the heavens, as separate from the earthly court, and that to each office a court has been assigned according to the quality of merits, a subject that was argued more fully earlier —; and this court, of which the discourse now is, had four little courts, one in each corner — which the Seventy call 'lesser ones' and we, for ease of sense, have called ὑποκοριστικῶς [in diminutive form] 'little courts' —: they were of forty cubits in length and thirty in breadth, numbers which I remember having discussed in this same prophet: that the one refers to tribulations and straits, the other to the perfect age — whence Moses and Elijah and the Lord and Savior fasted forty days in the desert; and they come to the priestly office not, as the Seventy have it, after the twenty-fifth year of age, but after the thirtieth, for which reason the Lord too was thirty years old when he came to baptism, and in this same prophet the thirtieth year is set at the beginning. Where, therefore, there is food, there are also the straits and the temptation through which food is procured; and when we have come to the age of the perfect man, there everything must be trodden underfoot, and one must say: Having food and clothing, with these we are content, and: If the Lord gives me food to eat and clothing to cover me, or surely that saying: Food for the belly and the belly for foods: but God will destroy both it and them; for in the future we shall not eat and drink, but shall feed on that bread: Which came down from heaven, of which it is sung in the psalter: Man will eat the bread of angels, and: My food is to do the will of him who sent me —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And that the four little courts which occupied the corners of the greater court were of one measure signifies the four quarters of the world: that we eat bread in the sweat of our face and all our labor profits the belly and the dung.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And these four little courts one wall also encircled: And kitchens were built beneath the porticoes all around, or they had couches nearby, so that where the food was, there was also the preparing of the tables.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And lest the prophet perhaps not know what he was seeing, he said to him: This is the house of the kitchens, in which the ministers of the Lord will cook the victims of the people: victims of the people indeed, which are offered for trespass or for sin and ignorance, but nourishment and refreshment for the priests, so that they may remember that they ought to desire nothing else, since even in the temple refreshments for their flesh have been prepared.

n: Waters. These waters are not to be understood literally, (for there were none such that flowed from the temple) but mystically of the baptism of Christ, and of his doctrine and his grace; the trees that grow on the banks are Christian virtues; the fishes are Christians, that spiritually live in and by these holy waters; the fishermen are the apostles, and apostolic preachers; the fenny places, where there is no health, are such as by being out of the Church are separated from these waters of life. (Challoner) --- It is not probable that real water or fishes were found, ver. 9. But this must be explained of the Church and of baptism, in a higher and more proper sense. (Worthington) --- Joel, (iii. 18.) before the captivity, and Zacharias, (xiv. 8.) after that event, speak of fountains as still to appear, and of course not in either temple, though Pilate made aqueducts for the purpose, (Josephus, Jewish Wars ii. 13.) which Tacitus, (An. v.) Maundrel, (p. 148.) and others mention. But the prophets allude not to them, but to Christ, the fountain of water springing up unto life eternal, John iv. 14., and vii. 38. (Calmet) --- Villalpand understands it of waters brought into the temple to wash the victims; but it seems to refer more to the grace and doctrine of Christ. (Menochius)
East. This gate was shut, and therefore he went out at the north gate. (Calmet)

The. Hebrew, "the east country," (Protestants; Haydock) or "the frontiers (Gelilah) eastward," by which some improperly suppose that one rivulet went to the sea of Galilee. --- And shall. Hebrew, "the sea of the going out," where the Jordan River empties itself into the Dead Sea; or, the second rivulet ran into the Mediterranean, Zacharias xiv. 8. But this passage relates to the Dead Sea alone, (ver. 18.) and Gelilah is a place near it, where the Israelites erected an altar of union, Josue xxii. 10. (Calmet) --- Healed. No fish can live in the sea of Sodom. (Solin xxxviii.) --- Yet, let the place be ever so noxious, this water shall cure it; (see 4 Kings ii. 19.; Calmet) which must be taken in a mystical sense. (Haydock)
Engallim, or "the fountain of Gallim," in the tribe of Benjamin, Isaias xxv. 44.
Salt, or bitumen pits. Schismatics and bad Christians, who do not live by the spirit of Christ, are meant. (Calmet)

First-fruits, or most excellent. (Haydock) --- St. John saw such (Worthington) a tree of life, Apocalypse xxii. (Haydock) --- The doctrine of the gospel, and the study of the sacred books, have the most salutary effects; while the very leaves, or the example of the saints, heal the soul. No more shall the deceitful fruits near Sodom be seen (Calmet) beautiful, but full of nothing but ashes. (Tacitus, An. v.) --- Where Christ instructs, a torrent of grace and glory is presently formed. Like the mustard seed growing into a large tree, in which the birds rest, its origin is mean; yet its progress is grand and astonishing.

Double portion. Literally, "cord." (Haydock) --- His two sons would each have a share, as Levi was better provided for. (Worthington) --- He had no portion of the land assigned to him by Josue, but here one part is appointed (Calmet) for the sacred ministers and the prince, chap. xlv. 1.

Brother.
