The seven tribes to the north have each an equal share, as the five who lay to the south of the Levites had with respect to each other, though their portion must have been only about half of what the former possessed, according to the map, chap. xlv. 1. (Haydock) --- Under Josue, the numbers of each tribe were considered. The present mysterious equality shews, perhaps, that there is no distinction of Jew or Gentile in the Church, and that Christ would come to redeem all. (Calmet) --- Lifted. People taking an oath acted in this manner. (Menochius)
Sedada. These places are not well known. They seem to be near the highest mountain specified, (Numbers xxxiv. 7.) west of Emesa.
Berotha, conquered by David, 2 Kings viii. 8.
Emath was about the middle of the northern limits, between the Mediterranean Sea and the Euphrates River.

Auran. Hence a line must be drawn through Damascus over Mount Galaad to the eastern or Dead Sea, to form the eastern borders. (Calmet) --- The Jordan River flowing from Genesareth to Sodom marked out this side, (Menochius) or rather was in this division; though the land as far as Galaad was to belong to Israel, as it had been before the captivity. Protestants, "by Jordan from the border unto," &c. (Haydock)
Thamar. Engaddi is sometimes understood: but it lay near Jericho, as this (Calmet) Thamar was to the south of the Dead Sea. (Ptolemy) --- Torrent Besor. (Haydock)

Emath, not that it was on the sea: but a line was to be drawn over against this city, eastward from the Mediterranean Sea. Septuagint, "to opposite the entrance of Emath, as far as its entrance." But the territory extended farther, Numbers xxxiv.

Strangers. This was never done by the Jews. It signifies that Christ would give an inheritance, in the true land of promise [in heaven], (Calmet) to all nations which should practice his religion, Romans x. 12. (Haydock)

f: The Epistle of Barnabas, Chapter XI

Further, what says He? "And there was a river flowing on the right, and from it arose beautiful trees; and whosoever shall eat of them shall live for ever." This meaneth, that we indeed descend into the water full of sins and defilement, but come up, bearing fruit in our heart, having the fear [of God] and trust in Jesus in our spirit. "And whosoever shall eat of these shall live for ever," This meaneth: Whosoever, He declares, shall hear thee speaking, and believe, shall live for ever.
LETTER 69.6
When the world falls into sin, nothing but a flood of waters can cleanse it again.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he turned me to the gate of the house, and behold, waters were going out beneath the threshold of the house toward the east; for the face of the house looked toward the east, and the waters were going down into the right side of the temple, to the south of the altar. And he led me out by the way of the gate of the north, and he turned me to the way outside, to the outer gate, the way that looked toward the east; and behold, waters overflowing from the right side. When the man who had a cord in his hand went out toward the east, he both measured a thousand cubits and led me across through the water up to the ankles (or he passed over in water, water of remission). And again he measured a thousand, and led me across through the water up to the knees (or and he passed over in water, water up to the thighs). And he measured a thousand, and led me across through the water up to the kidneys (or and he passed over the water up to the loins). And he measured a thousand, a torrent which I could not pass across, for the deep waters of the torrent had swelled, which could not be forded (for which the Seventy translated: And he measured a thousand, and he could not pass across, for the water was borne along like a headlong torrent which cannot be crossed). These waters which were going out beneath the threshold of the house, that is, of the temple, were not borne toward the north and toward the west but toward the east and on the right side of the temple, that is, toward the south, and that south not of just any place, but of the altar — from which it becomes clear that the waters are sacred and signify the teaching of our Savior, according to that which is written: Out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and in another place: All things have been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as much water covering the sea; of these waters the prophet Zechariah too prophesied, saying: On that day living water shall go out from Jerusalem, and the middle of it into the first sea, and the middle of it into the last sea; of these waters the Lord too spoke to the Samaritan woman: If you knew who it is who says to you: Give me to drink, you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water, and again: Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst forever, and in the temple he cried out and said: If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly. But this he said of the Spirit whom those who believed in him were to receive; these are the waters of which the prophet spoke in the psalm: Beside the water of refreshment he has brought me up, and in Ezekiel: I will take you from the nations and from the lands, and I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleannesses. For there appeared the springs of waters, and in Psalm 92 (93) it is sung: The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices. From the voices of many waters, wonderful are the swellings of the sea; these are: The waters of Shiloah that go with silence, of which Isaiah speaks: You shall draw waters from the springs of the Savior, and the psalmist: Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel, and the same Isaiah of the Lord Savior: He, he says, shall dwell in a lofty cave of the strongest rock; bread shall be given him, and his water is faithful. For water has broken forth in the desert, and a valley in a thirsty land, and it is said to believers: Fear not, for I have redeemed you; you are mine. And if you pass through water, I am with you, and again: You who thirst, go to the water; and through Jeremiah God speaks: For my people has done evil things: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns, which cannot hold water. Just as, then, we read in a good sense the waters which go out from the threshold of the temple and are referred to the teaching of the Church, so there are bitter waters and most evil waters which the prophet Jeremiah forbids us to approach, saying: What have you to do with the way of Egypt, that you should drink of the waters of 'Geon'? — which in Hebrew is called 'Sior', that is, 'turbid' and 'muddy' —, of which God, angered over the heretics, speaks: Behold, I will feed them with distresses, and I will give them water of gall to drink; in which the Egyptian dragon reigns, who says: The rivers are mine, and I made them, who: Sees every high thing, and he himself is king of those who are in the waters; whence the man of the Church entreats the Lord and says: Save me, O Lord, for the waters have come in even to my soul. I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance; I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me, and again: May I be delivered from those who hate me and from the depth of the waters. Let not the tempest of water cast me down, nor the deep swallow me up; nor let the pit press its mouth upon me, and in another psalm: Unless the Lord had been among us, let Israel now say, unless the Lord had been among us, when men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive; when their fury was angered against us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us up, and the bride in the Song of Songs: Much water will not be able to quench love, and rivers will not overwhelm it; this is the water of which Hosea says: Gilead has despised me, the city that works vanities, troubling the water, and its strength pirate men; which water is called by another name 'merra', that is, 'bitterness' — into which the wood of the Cross is cast, and bitter things are turned into sweet —; consider the law of Moses, if it is understood according to the carnal sense of the Jews, how bitter it is — digging out: An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth —: the fornication of Judah with Tamar, and Hosea joined to a harlot, Jeremiah's περίζωμα [loincloth], Moses' Ethiopian wife, the killing of the Egyptian, and a thousand other things which, if we understand them according to the letter that kills and not according to the spirit that gives life, are bitter and do not so much edify their reader as destroy him —. These waters, then, which go out from the temple of the Lord, proceed toward the east and go down into the right side of the temple, to the south of the altar, where the bridegroom feeds his guests and reclines.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But what follows: And he led me out by the way of the gate of the north, and turned to the way outside, to the outer gate, the way that looked toward the east, secretly shows that we cannot come at once to the eastern gate unless we come to it by the way of the gate of the north, by a long circuit: for unless we overcome the coldest wind by the heat of faith and trample its regions — so that that apostolic saying may be fulfilled in us: But God will crush Satan under your feet swiftly —, we are not able to enter the gate through which the waters enter and are on the right side; and note that these waters, which go out through the gate of the east, flee the left-hand parts to such a degree that they are described as proceeding from the right of the altar toward the south.
Commentary on Ezekiel

'But that man who had the cord in his hand, when he had led me through the gate of the north, outside, to the way that looked toward the east, and he himself too was in the same place, measured a thousand cubits of the same water'. And he led me across through the water up to the 'ankles' — which Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated ἀστραγάλους [anklebones] — (for which the Seventy translated: But he passed over in water, water of remission), which we can understand to signify the first sins of men, which are remitted to us as we enter the waters of the Lord, and they show the saving grace of baptism, and are the beginnings of progress; finally, they reach as far as the ankles, which are neighbors to the sole and the heel — which lies open to the bites of the snake, as the Lord says: You shall watch for his head, and he shall watch for your heel; and in the Psalter it is said of Judas the betrayer: He who ate my bread has magnified tripping-up against me (or the heel: for this is what the Greek πτέρνα means).
Commentary on Ezekiel

And after the thousand cubits which reach as far as the ankle: He measured another thousand cubits in the water and led me across up to the knees: since after the remission of sins and the beginnings of progress, when we strive to climb a little from earthly things to higher ones, we bend the knees to the Lord — as the Apostle says: That every knee should bend, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father —. Thirdly: He measured a thousand cubits, and led me, he says, across through the water up to the kidneys: for by these steps we come to the heights, which heights themselves, however, reach up to the loins and kidneys, so that all lust in us may be cut off, and we may possess the sanctification of the body without which no one will see God — whence also in this same prophet God is seen fiery from the feet up to the loins: for the works of the loins need fire and purgation, as the righteous man says: For my loins have been filled with illusions, through which the enemy mocks us both by day and in the phantasm of the nights; but from the loins up to the head and crown he shines with the brilliance of electrum, the most precious metal, so that he has in himself nothing of filth, nothing of baseness —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Whence now fourthly it is said: And he measured a thousand, 'cubits' being understood, a torrent — which the Seventy did not translate —, which I could not pass across (much better than the Seventy, who said: which he could not pass across): for the prophet, and all human nature, cannot after the loins pass across the torrent of thoughts and the incitements of vices; but that man: Who was clothed in 'baddi' [linen], and the guide of the prophet, clearly passes across: Who did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth. And he gives the reasons why the prophet could not pass across the fourth thousand cubits: For, he says, the deep waters of the torrent had swelled, which cannot be forded — and how is it written, with the prophet glorying: Our soul has passed across the torrent? But it is easily resolved if we know that in place of this it is written in the Hebrew: The torrent has passed across my soul —. Of this torrent Isaiah too speaks: Behold, I incline upon them like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent glory, and in Psalm 35 (36) it is said of the saints: In the protection of your wings they will hope, they will be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and with the torrent of your delights you will give them drink; for with you is the fountain of life, and in Psalm 124 (125): Turn back, O Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south, and of the Savior: He will drink of the torrent on the way — for who of men can boast that he has a chaste heart?, or: Into whose mind has the death of concupiscence not entered through the windows of the eyes and, to say little, a tickling of the soul? For the world is set in the evil one, and: From childhood the heart of man is set on evil, so that from the very beginning of birth the human condition is not without sin for even a single day; whence David too confesses in the psalm: 'For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me, not by the iniquities of my mother or indeed my own, but in the iniquities of the human condition'; whence the Apostle too says: Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam —. That we say 'cubitos' [cubits] in the masculine gender and not, according to the rule of the grammarians, in the neuter 'cubita', I have also taught above: that we do this not from ignorance but from custom, for the sake also of the simple and unlearned, whose number in the congregation of the Church is the greater.
Commentary on Ezekiel

That man, who was Ezekiel's guide, admonishes the prophet to look more carefully and see, and to attend with the eyes of the mind to hidden mysteries; and he calls him 'son of man' either as a figure of the Lord Savior — for 'Hiezechiel' means 'strength' or 'dominion of God' —, or certainly as a reminder of human frailty — lest he forget his condition while great things are shown to him —; and having admonished him he leads him and turns him to the bank of the torrent so that, since he could not cross the middle depth, he might at least recognize the things that are on the banks.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And he said to me: Surely you have seen, son of man; and he led me out, and turned me to the bank of the torrent (or of the river). And when I had turned (or he had turned me), behold, on the bank of the torrent (or of the river) a great many trees (or very many trees) on either side; and he said to me: These waters, which go out to the mounds of sand of the east and go down to the plains of the desert (or this water which goes out into Galilee, which slopes toward the east, and goes down to Arabia), will enter the sea; and they will go out, and the waters will be healed: and every living soul (or of animals) that creeps (or of creeping things), wherever the torrent (or the river) comes, will live, and there will be very many fish after these waters have come there, and all things will be healed and will live to which the torrent (or the river) comes. And fishermen will stand over them from En-gedi to En-eglaim; there will be a drying of nets; very many kinds of its fish there will be, like the fish of the great sea, of exceeding multitude. But in the places that go out beyond the banks and are marshy they will not be healed, but will be given over to salt-pits. And over the torrent (or river) there will rise on its banks on either side every fruit tree (or fruit-bearing tree); its leaf will not fall from it (or nothing will grow old from it), and its fruit will not fail: each month it will bring forth early fruits (or all things will be renewed), because its waters will go out from the sanctuary, and its fruit will be for food, and its leaves for medicine (or and its ascent for health). I wished to set down the whole passage together, although it is lengthy, so as not to break in upon the sense of the reader, and so that the order of the reading, divided into parts, might not confuse the understanding of the hearer. And first it must be said that for 'torrent', which in Hebrew is called 'nehel' and in the Greek tongue is named χειμάρρος, the Seventy translated 'river'; next, that for 'Galilee', which in Hebrew is called 'galila', Aquila translated θινάς, which means 'mounds' 'of sand', Symmachus μεθόριον, which we can translate 'border-region'; for 'Arabia' too Symmachus translated 'uninhabitable', Aquila 'low places' or 'plains', Theodotion 'arabas' [a transliteration of the Hebrew word]. Let us say, then, what seems right to us in each point.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And when, he says, I had turned (or he had turned me, who was guide and admonisher), behold, on the bank of the torrent (or of the river) many trees (or a great many trees) exceedingly, on either side: this 'torrent', which on account of the abundance of its waters is borne along in the manner of a torrent and receives rains from heaven, of which we spoke in the preceding reading, is itself called by the Seventy 'river', because it has perpetual waters, not collected from rains here and there but abiding from a living and perpetual spring — of which river we read many things in the holy scriptures, but for the present a few things must be said, and first that: The rush of the river makes glad the city of God, and in another place: The river of God is filled with waters; you have prepared their food, for so is your preparation, and again in the plural: The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices. From the voices of many waters, wonderful are the swellings of the sea, and in Isaiah: I will make a way in the desert, and rivers in the pathless place, and in another place of the same it will appear more plainly that in Zion a river runs down, glorious in a thirsty land —; above this river there were very many trees on either side of the bank, so that, namely, the river ran enclosed between the two instruments, the old and the new; and the many trees, or the very many and exceedingly numerous trees, I take to be those which scripture records in paradise as abounding with various fruits.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the guide who goes before, the teacher, teaches the prophet and says: These waters, which go out (or into Galilee of the nations according to the Seventy, or, as is more truly contained in the Hebrew:) to the mounds of sand of the east and go down to the plains of the desert (or to Arabia), will enter the sea (or to the outlets of the sea), and the waters will be healed; we said long ago that the waters signify either the grace of baptism or the teaching of the Gospel, which, if they go out from the threshold of the temple of the Lord and hold to the apostolic discipline, make the mounds of sand, previously sterile and unfruitful, to be fruit-bearing, and so water all the plains and deserts as to express among themselves too the mystery of the spring of Jericho — which Elisha healed with the evangelic and apostolic salt, to such a degree that where there had previously been sterility and death, there was fertility and life —; nor did they heal the deserts only, but they enter the eastern sea — namely the 'Dead' sea, in which nothing living could exist, and the 'most bitter' sea, which in Greek they call λίμνην ἀσφαλτῖτιν, that is, 'lake of bitumen' —; and in a wonderful manner the dead waters are healed by the waters of the Gospel — which, from the fact that they have nothing living in them, have obtained the name of death: for they did not know him who says: I am the life; and in truth, according to the letter, up to now nothing that breathes and can move about can be found in this sea because of its excessive bitterness: not even little snails and small worms and eels and the other kinds of animals or creeping things whose little bodies we can know better than their names; finally, if the Jordan, swollen by rains, flowing in there, has carried fish along, they die at once and float on the fat waters —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Since, then, these waters have nothing of usefulness, as the plain account testifies, even if it should come about, as the foolish superstition of the Jews believes, according to the spiritual understanding, healed by the torrent of the Lord, they will have very many fish, and all things to which this torrent comes will live, so that fishermen stand over the banks from 'Engaddi' to 'Engallim' — of which the first means 'spring' or 'eye' 'of the kid', the next 'spring, or eye' 'of calves': En-eglaim is at the beginning of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan enters, and En-gedi where it ends and is consumed; and I think the Dead Sea is the one of which Zechariah speaks: On that day living water will go out from Jerusalem, and the middle of it into the first sea; Daniel too agrees with these words: I was seeing, and behold, the four winds of heaven were rushing into the great sea, and David: Wonderful, he says, are the upliftings of the sea, and in the person of the Savior in the psalm: I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me; the king of Egypt too, according to this same Ezekiel, is called a dragon who dwells in the sea and fans the rivers as with his horns, and again: This great and spacious sea; which, as long as it has not received into itself the water of the river or torrent, kills everything it has in itself: but the Lord — of whom it was said: He will strike: and he will heal after two days, and on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight — himself speaks in the same prophet Hosea: I bound Ephraim, I took him up in my arm, and they did not know that I healed them in the corruption of men — he who: Was wounded for our sins and made weak for our iniquities; the discipline of his peace is upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed —; he himself healed by his death this sea, which is most salty and dead from excessive bitterness, he who says through Isaiah: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to heal those who are contrite of heart, whence through Jeremiah too he cries out: Turn back, you turning sons, and I will heal your contritions — for the people, impatient and not enduring to bear the pain of its wounds any longer, had said: The summer has passed, the harvest has gone by, and we are not saved, whence the Lord also answered it: Is there no resin in Gilead, or are there no physicians there? Why has the healing of my people not gone up? —, and Jeremiah himself cries aloud and says: Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me and I shall be saved; finally the angels — who were the guardians of the Jews at that time when the foolish multitude cried out and said: His blood be upon us and upon our children, and the veil of the temple was torn and all the mysteries of the Hebrews were laid open — answered the Lord who commanded them, and said: We have treated Babylon and she is not healed; let us leave her, namely the city of confusion and of vices — whence Josephus too relates in his History that, after the Lord was crucified and the veil of the temple was torn, or the lintel of the temple broke and fell, a voice of the heavenly powers was heard in the inner shrines of the temple: Let us pass over from these seats —. Let all this have been said not superfluously but necessarily, because the Dead Sea is said to have been healed when the river of the Lord flowed into it —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Over this sea — from 'Engaddi', 'the eye and spring of the kid', which is always offered for sins, up to 'Engallim', 'the spring of calves', which are slaughtered to the Lord and imitate the calf that puts forth horns and hoofs, which are slaughtered at the altar in type of the Savior — there will be fishermen, to whom Jesus speaks: Come to me and I will make you fishermen, of whom Jeremiah too: Behold, I, he says, will send fishermen; and very many species, or rather kinds, of fish will be in the sea once dead, which fish Peter drew out on the right-hand side at the Lord's command, and they were one hundred and fifty-three, so that the nets were breaking because of their multitude — and those who have written on the natures of animals, and especially those who have published ἁλιευτικά [works on fishing] in the Latin as well as the Greek tongue — of whom Opianicus the Cilician is a most learned poet —, say that there are one hundred and fifty-three kinds of fish; all of which were caught by the apostles, and nothing remained uncaught, while both noble and ignoble, both rich and poor, and every kind of men is drawn out of the sea of this world to salvation —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But what follows: On its shores and in the marshy places (or in those which go out from the shore) the waters will not be healed, secretly shows that whoever was not in Noah's ark perishes while the flood reigns, and that those whom this river has not touched do not receive healing: But they will be given, he says, to salt-pits, according to that which is written: When the pestilent man is scourged, the fool will be wiser — for the examples of the worse instruct the good —, or: They will be given to salt-pits, according to that which is written in the Gospel: Salt is good; but if the salt has become foolish, it is useful for nothing, so that they may lack crops and greenness forever — which a city too, sprinkled with salt after its ruin, demonstrates —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But over the torrent (or the river) there will rise on its banks on either side every fruit tree (or, as all have translated with one voice, βρώσιμον, 'that which provides food and nourishment' and 'that which can be eaten'; and in the Hebrew tongue it is called 'machal'). And: (nothing, according to the Seventy, will grow old in it, but its produce will be renewed daily, or:) its leaf will not fall from it, and its fruit will not fail, according to that which is written in Psalm 1: And he will be like the tree that is planted beside the runnings of waters, which will give its fruit in its season; and its leaf will not fall. Each month, he says, it will bring forth early fruits (or, as is written in the Seventy: its fruit in its renewal will give early fruits), so that all the fruits of believers may be firstfruits and the single months may be assigned to the single apostles; and this will come about: Because its waters will go out from the sanctuary: lest we think that so great an abundance of produce belongs to the banks or the trees or the months, he gives the causes of the fertility and adds: Because its waters will go out from the sanctuary — So then it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy —. The primacy among all these trees is held by the tree of life, which is understood as wisdom, of which it is written: She is a tree of life to all who believe in her. That which is said: And its fruit will be for food, and its leaf for medicine, shows the mysteries of the divine books, of which the one pertains to the letter, the other to the spirit, so that we understand the simple words in the leaves, but in the fruits the hidden sense: for just as the knowledge of the scriptures leads to the kingdoms of heaven and offers us the bread who says: I am the bread who came down from heaven, so its leaves, which contain moral teaching, bestow health, so as to heal the wounds of those who sin. For 'leaves', which in Hebrew are called 'ale', the Seventy, on account of the likeness of the word and of the sound, translated 'ascent', which itself too can be explained thus: that, after the food of the fruits, we may climb by the admonitions of the words to heavenly things.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Thus says the Lord God. This is the boundary by which you shall possess the land in the twelve tribes of Israel, because Joseph has a double cord; and you shall possess it — each one equally as his brother — the land which I lifted up my hand to give to your fathers; and this land shall fall to you as a possession. In place of what we said: Because Joseph has a double cord, the Seventy translated: Increase of the cord — for 'Ioseph' means 'increase —, understanding a thing in place of a name and confusing the mind of the reader: for when the Levitical tribe had been subtracted and assigned to the sacrifices of the temple, there remained eleven tribes, of which Joseph was divided into two, Ephraim and Manasseh, who said to Joshua son of Nun: Why have you given me a possession of one lot and one cord, though I am of so great a multitude and the Lord has blessed me?, to whom Joshua answered: If you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and cut down spaces for yourself in the land of the Perizzite and of Rephaim, since the possession of mount Ephraim is narrow for you, and again: And Joshua said to the house of Ephraim and Manasseh: You are a numerous people and of great strength; you shall not have one lot, but you shall pass over to the mountain and cut down and clear for yourself spaces for dwelling; and you will be able to proceed further when you have overthrown the Canaanite, who you say has iron chariots and is very strong; I have said this for this reason, because scripture now records that Joseph, that is, Ephraim and Manasseh, has a double cord.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the individual tribes receive equal spaces of land according to their multitude, by no means at the discretion of the one dividing but by lot, which rests in the power of the Lord. Finally Joshua himself too, who was the divider of the land, did not set apart his own land for himself, lest he should seem to have chosen the best, but received from the princes of all the tribes: Timnath-serah in mount Ephraim.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And this is the boundary of the land: toward the northern quarter, from the Great Sea, by the way of Ethalon, for those coming to Sadada, Hamath, Berotha, Sabarim, which is between the middle of Damascus and the border of Hamath, the court of Thicon, which is beside Hauran (or of Auranitis); and the boundary shall be from the sea up to 'the court of Enom' (or 'Aser-Enan'), the boundary of Damascus; and from north to north the boundary of Hamath, the northern quarter. Between the description of the holy land of the twelve tribes by Joshua son of Nun and the one which is now commanded to be made through Ezekiel there is this difference: that there the land is divided among the tribes by lot, here it is assigned by the discretion of the Lord who commands. In the book of Numbers, then, in which the whole land of promise is divided by four quarters in brief speech, this is the description from the north, that is, from the northern quarter: Moreover, on the northern side the boundaries will begin from the Great Sea, reaching as far as the Highest Mountain, from which you will come into Hamath, up to the borders of Sedada. And the borders will go as far as Zephrona and 'the village of Enan' (or 'Aser-Enan'). And the Hebrews say that the northern quarter begins from the Great Sea, which stretches along the shores of Palestine, of Phoenicia, and of the Syria which is called Coele, and of Cilicia, and extends through Egypt to Libya. But as to what he says: Reaching — the boundaries — as far as the Highest Mountain, the same Hebrews assert that it signifies either Mount Amanus or the Taurus — which seems truer to us —. From which, he says, you will come into 'Emath', which is now named 'Epiphania', its name having been changed by Antiochus, the cruelest of tyrants, for he had the surname Ἐπιφανής [Epiphanes, the Manifest]. Up to the borders, he says, of Sedada, which place is also set down in the present reading of Ezekiel. And the borders will go as far as Zephrona, which city they today call Zephyrium, a town of Cilicia. And what follows: And 'the village of Enan' (for which in the Hebrew is written 'Aser-Enon' or '-Enan'), the present passage also contains. And meanwhile let it suffice to have touched on it briefly according to the history and to have joined side by side the description both of Numbers and of Ezekiel, so that the prudent reader may understand in which points they record either the same or neighboring or different things; now, having interpreted the names of each, let us follow the ἀναγωγήν [anagogy, the higher sense], and let us set out, the Lord granting it, what seems right to us in each point. 'Ethalon' means 'cradle of grief'; 'Sedada', 'his side' — understand it from 'side', not from 'breadth'; 'Emath', 'fury', which in Greek is called χόλος; 'Berotha', 'wells'; 'Sabarim', 'circuit of mountains'; 'Damascus', 'blood of sackcloth' and 'of a kiss' or 'of a cup'; but the 'house' or 'court of Thicon' Symmachus translates 'the middle court', which goes on to the borders of 'Auran'; therefore 'Thicon' means 'middle'; 'Auran' — which the Seventy turned into the Greek tongue as 'Auranitis' —, 'wrath'; but 'Asar' '-Enon' — which is the boundary of Damascus — is called in our language 'court of the spring'. The northern quarter, then, begins from the Great Sea and goes by the way of 'Ethalon', which means 'cradle of grief'; through penitence it comes to 'Sadada', where there is a turning aside 'from the side': for we understand 'Emath', that is, the 'indignation' of God, impending over us, or, 'Emath' having been found to be 'truth', the 'wells' of 'Berotha' are opened to us, which the princes Abraham, Isaac and Jacob dug, and by a long 'circuit' we come to the 'mountains' of 'Sabarim', which are set between 'Damascus', that is, 'the blood of haircloth', and the border of 'Emath', that is, as we said above, 'of truth' — for just as through grief we turn aside impending evils and avoid them from the side, so after the blood and haircloth of a bloody life, before we come to the borders of Emath, we go around and come to the mountains of which it is written: Mountains round about it, and the Lord round about his people —, which place is called 'the court of Thicon', that is, 'the middle court', as Symmachus translated, beside the borders of 'Auran', which means 'wrath' — so that we may say with the prophet: I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him —, and from the sea up to the borders of Damascus: in which the apostle Paul too, from Jewish fury and the shedding of the Church's blood, beheld the light through blindness and, having taken up the haircloth for his old persecution, preached the Gospel, so that he might come to the eternal 'court of the spring' and, once set in the north, might lay hold of the boundary of truth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the eastern quarter, from the midst of Hauran and from the midst of Damascus and from the midst of Gilead and from the midst of the land of Israel, the Jordan dividing, to the eastern sea; you shall measure the eastern quarter. For which in the book of Numbers I have found it written thus: Thence they shall measure the boundaries toward the eastern quarter from 'the village of Enan' (that is, 'Aser-Enon') as far as Sephama, and from Sephama the boundaries will go down to Rebla, opposite the spring; thence they will come toward the east to the sea of Chinnereth, and they will extend as far as the Jordan, and at the last they will be closed by the sea. Above he had said: And the boundary shall be from the sea up to Eser-Enon, the boundary of Damascus: from the end of the northern quarter, then, that is, from the court of Enan, the boundaries extend according to the book of Numbers as far as Sephama, which the Hebrews name Apamea, and from Apamea the boundaries will go down to Rebla, which is now called Antioch of Syria; and so that you may know that this Rebla signifies the city which is now the most renowned in Coele-Syria, there follows: Opposite the spring, which it is evident signifies Daphne, from which spring the aforesaid city enjoys most abundant waters — this place was planted by the military hand of Gnaeus Pompey, who first subjected Judea to Roman rule, and from him — following the fable of the poets — it received the name of Daphne, on account of the laurels and cypresses, trees which are very frequent in that very place too —. Thence, he says, the boundaries will come toward the eastern quarter to the sea of Chinnereth: as far as the lake of Tiberias; and it is called a sea although it has sweet waters, according to the idiom of the scriptures, which call gatherings of waters seas. And the boundaries, he says, will extend as far as the Jordan, and at the last will be closed by the sea: either by the Dead Sea or, as others think, by the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Aila is situated, where a legion and garrison of the Romans is now stationed. Let this have been said according to the book of Numbers. But according to Ezekiel: from the midst of Hauran, which is a town of Damascus in the wilderness, and from the midst of Gilead, which, a mountain joined to the hills of Lebanon, fell into the lot of Reuben and Gad and of the half tribe of Manasseh, and is behind Phoenicia and Arabia — to which mountain Jacob came, having set out from Carrhae, and was overtaken by Laban; of which Jeremiah too speaks: Gilead, you are to me the beginning of Lebanon; which Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, took from the region of the Amorites —; and the end of this quarter: the river Jordan bounding it, and the eastern sea, which in this place they understand as the Dead Sea, not the tongue of the Red Sea. Let us speak according to tropology. After the boundaries of the north, by a long circuit through Ethalon and Sedada and Berotha, Sabarim too and Thicon and Auran and Damascus and the court of Enom, the eastern quarter reaches as far as Emath: from the midst of the 'wrath' of 'Auran', and from the midst of 'Damascus', namely of the 'blood' 'of penitence', and from the midst of 'Galaad', which means 'revelation' or 'mound of testimony': so that, after wrath and penitence, it may show the hope of salvation; and from the midst of the land of 'Israel', which contains the 'vision' 'of peace', it reaches to the most sweet streams of the Jordan, which, with the sea set far apart, attains the light of the east, so that it is ended by the 'river' 'Iordanis', which means 'stream of judgment', and by the boundary of the 'torrent'; but what is set down in the Seventy, 'phoeniconos', that is, 'of the palm grove', is not found in the Hebrew, for which we translated 'you shall measure': and the error is manifest, because for 'thamoddu' [you shall measure], deceived by the likeness of the letters 'daleth' and 'res' [d and r], they read 'thamorru' [palm].
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the southern quarter, the meridional, from Tamar up to the waters of contradiction (or to the waters of 'Mariboth' — for these mean 'contradiction' or διαδίκασμοι, that is, 'disputes' —) of Kadesh too, and the torrent up to the Great Sea; this is the southern quarter toward the south. For which in the book of Numbers it is written thus: It will begin from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and will have as boundaries toward the east the sea. And they will go around the southern quarter by the Ascent of the Scorpion, so that they pass Senna and come into the south as far as Kadesh-barnea, whence the borders will go out to a village named Addar, and will extend as far as Asemona. And the boundary will go around from Asemona as far as the torrent of Egypt, and will be ended by the shore of the Great Sea. Which briefly signifies this — lest on the occasion of Ezekiel we seem to pass over to a very broad exposition of Numbers —: that the boundary goes around from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and from the Red Sea, and, through the Ascent of the Scorpion and through Senna and Kadesh-barnea and the court of Addar and Asemona, reaches as far as the torrent of Egypt, which flows into the sea beside the city of Rhinocorura; but this boundary of the southern quarter, that is, the meridional, begins from Tamar — which is a city in the wilderness, which Solomon too built with wondrous works, and today it is named Palmyra, and in the Hebrew tongue it is called 'thamar', which in our language means 'palm' — up to the waters of contradiction of Kadesh, which beyond doubt is in the desert, and the torrent entering the Great Sea, this sea which stretches along the shores of Egypt and Palestine, and this is the southern quarter toward the south. After the quarter of the north, then, and of the east, when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, we receive the meridional quarter, when the whole light is poured upon us from above, and with Abraham we enter the banquet and are inebriated with wine — which makes glad the heart of man — with Joseph and his brothers; and this possession and these boundaries begin from 'Thamar', namely from the 'palm' and the victory over vices, up to the waters of contradiction: for virtues are always contradicted — whence the Jews too, disputing against Paul, assert that the preaching of the Gospel is contradicted in the whole world; and in the Gospel we read, as Simeon says: This one will be for the ruin and resurrection of many, and for a sign that will be contradicted —, but all contradiction is of 'holiness', which 'Cades' means — as the psalmist says: The Lord will shake the desert of Cades: which, namely, at first did not have the holiness of the Lord, but was shaken and moved, so as to receive God as its guest, who says: Upon whom will my spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet and the one who trembles at my words? —; after the desert of Cades, up to the Great Sea, in the south of the southern quarter, is the torrent of which we spoke above, which has rains not from the earth but from heaven, collected from the variety of diverse virtues.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the quarter of the sea, the Great Sea, from the border straight on until you come to Hamath; this is the quarter of the sea. Of which the book of Numbers writes more plainly and more briefly: But the western quarter will begin from the Great Sea, and will be closed by that same end, that is, from sea to sea: namely from the torrent of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, up to that place which is opposite Hamath, the city of Syria, of which we spoke above. But the west, according to the laws of tropology, is always in the sea, always in the brine and the waves, where every day shipwrecks are stirred up, and the deaths of the wretched, and the loss of riches and merchandise; and yet, when we have broken all these things by patience, we come straight on to 'Emath', that is, to the 'truth' of the Lord, who, once persecutions are overcome, has promised us eternal rewards.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And you shall divide this land for yourselves by the tribes of Israel; and you shall cast it as an inheritance, for yourselves and for the strangers who have come to you, who will have begotten sons in your midst, and they shall be to you as natives among the sons of Israel: with you they shall divide the possession in the midst of the tribes of Israel; and in whatever tribe the stranger shall be, there you shall give him a possession, says the Lord God. Through this passage we learn — and the haughtiness of the Jews is struck down — that nothing is divided between Israel and the people of the Gentiles: for if the land is divided to strangers and foreigners together with those who are of the people of Israel, that is, the natives, no one doubts that the inheritance is the same for the people of the Gentiles and for the people of the Jews, if only they have been converted to the worship of the God of Israel — which properly possesses the name Christian —, the Jews having the letter of the law and we the spirit, they holding the parchments and we him who is written in the parchments; and with Moses the land is divided by lot, but here, as we said, it is assigned by the judgment of the Lord, and there is one possession for the stranger and for Israel, and in the individual tribes the inheritance is given, at the command of the Lord God.

n: Dan. This division is very different from that of Josue, and was never literally executed, being rather of a mystical nature. The limits are not marked out, as each lot was equal. (Calmet) See chap. xlv. 1., and xlvii. 14. (Haydock) --- By the twelve tribes all the glorified saints are meant. No cities of refuge occur, because in heaven all are perfect, all secure. (St. Jerome) (Worthington)

Apart, for the Levitical tribe and the prince. (Calmet) --- As the first-born and things which spring first, so also the land consecrated to the Lord is called first-fruits. (Worthington) --- Thousand cubits (chap. xlv. 1.) or 12,500 paces, (Haydock) allowing two cubits for each. This would not reach to the Jordan River. But thrice that space must be reckoned, the king having two of them (Calmet) on each side of the temple, namely, towards the sea, and on the other side of the Jordan. (Haydock)

Astray, &c. By this we see, that in the worst of times God always preserved some of the priests from going astray; and that the synagogue never fell so universally into idolatry, but that a remnant was still left free from this corruption. (Challoner)
Ten. Their city was only 18,000 cubits in circumference, ver. 16.
Profane, where servants of the priests may reside. (Calmet) --- On the north and south, (Haydock) 1000 cubits broad and 25,000 long were left for fields, gardens, &c. (Calmet)

Five. Hebrew has, "five five hundred:" but one five is properly omitted in several manuscripts and in all the ancient versions. (Kennicott) --- Four thousand five hundred cubits was the length and breadth of the town and temple, which were 18,000 cubits round, (Calmet) or so many reeds, which would make 36 miles of 1000 paces each. As the earthly Jerusalem was certainly never so large, the modern rabbins assert that the Messias will build it to that extent; but Catholic doctors understand it mystically of the Church. Thus St. John saw the New Jerusalem or Church triumphant [in heaven], Apocalypse xxi., and xxii. (Worthington)
Suburbs, separating the Levites from laics, different from what is mentioned [in] ver. 15.
As the, &c. They shall not be alienated, as some might infer from its being said to be profane, which term is used because it was the habitation of laymen.

Israel. People from all parts might serve the Levites. This tribe was not to engage in labourious or sordid employments, being attached to the service of the Lord, and bound to instruct others. But this was more perfectly fulfilled in the Christian Church, where the clergy enjoy great immunities, and are forbidden to exercise any trade or employment which may take them off from their more important spiritual concerns, or render their ministry contemptible. See Exodus xix. 6.
City, where the Levites and their servants, artisans, &c., dwelt. (Calmet)

Thereof. The domains of the prince touched the limits of Juda on the north, and of Benjamin on the south, as the portion of Levi did also. The prince occupied the east and west square of this division. (Haydock)

Inheritance. Hebrew nachal, signifies also "torrent;" and St. Jerome seems to prefer this meaning, as he explains it of the torrent which goes by Rhinocorura, and is commonly supposed to be the southern boundary. (Calmet)
Out, or gates. (Haydock) --- There were three on each of the four sides. (Calmet)

The Lord is there. This name is here given to the city; that is, the Church of Christ; because the Lord is always with her till the end of the world, Matthew xxviii. 20. (Challoner) --- He always adorns the Church triumphant [in heaven]; (Apocalypse xxii.) but has deserted the synagogue, Matthew xxiii. 38. (Worthington) --- Jerusalem certainly never bore this name, nor is it requisite that she should, if the prophecy had been literally understood. It would suffice, if she could justly claim such a prerogative. See Isaias vii. 14., and 2 Kings xii. 25. The Church of Christ possesses God for ever. (Calmet)

f: Commentary on Ezekiel

And these are the names of the tribes: from the borders of the north, beside the way of Ethalon, for those going to Hamath, Court Enon, the border of Damascus toward the north beside Hamath; and its eastern side shall be the sea, Dan one. And from the border of Dan, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Asher one. And above the border of Asher, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Naphtali one. And above the border of Naphtali, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Manasseh one. And above the border of Manasseh, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Ephraim one. And above the border of Ephraim, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Reuben one. And above the border of Reuben, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Judah one. Now that the possession of the holy land has been described, both according to the present prophecy of Ezekiel and according to the book of Numbers, the possession of the individual tribes is now described, from the eastern side to the side of the west, that is, of the sea. And first they receive their boundaries from the north, beside the way of Ethalon, for those going to Hamath, 'Court' — or 'Aser' — Enon, the border of Damascus toward the north beside Hamath, of which we have already spoken before; and the tribe of Dan begins first, Asher second, Naphtali third, Manasseh fourth, Ephraim fifth, Reuben sixth, Judah seventh: that is, on the left side, and the number seven is completed. — Then the firstfruits of the priests and of the Levites, and the sanctuary of the Lord in the midst, and the Holy of Holies; the city itself also is described, foursquare, having four thousand and five hundred reeds on each side; the suburbs of the priests and of the Levites are also described in order, and the possession of the prince; and again on the right side follow five tribes, likewise from the side of the east to the side of the west, of which the first is Benjamin, the second Simeon, having its own possession specially and by no means mixed with Judah as before, the third Issachar, the fourth Zebulun, the fifth Gad; and the gates of the city, three on each side, and the name of the city itself, which is contained on the plate of gold on the forehead of the high priest — about all of which we shall discourse in their places —. This too is to be noted: that the names of the forty-eight cities which in the volume of Numbers are given to the Levitical tribe to dwell in, with their suburbs, are passed over in silence here, and so are the cities of the fugitives, of which three beyond the Jordan, namely Bezer and Ramoth and Golan, were given in the two and a half tribes, and three on this side of the Jordan, namely Kedesh and Shechem and Kiriath-arba: for there was no need, in a mystical description and in the dwelling of the saints and a perfect way of life, to describe the refuges of fugitives, which Israel needed while still set upon the earth and hastening through many labors and dangers to come to this city, and saying in each of the saints: I am a stranger and a sojourner, as all my fathers were, and in another place: I have dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar; much has my soul sojourned.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And above the border of Judah, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, shall be the firstfruits which you shall set apart, twenty-five thousand in breadth, and in length as each of the portions from the eastern side to the side of the sea; and the sanctuary shall be in the midst of it. The firstfruits which you shall set apart for the Lord: the length twenty-five thousand, and the breadth ten thousand. It is superfluous to discuss again what has been discussed, and to labor once more, as though they had not been said, over things on which we labored above. After the boundaries of the seven tribes, the firstfruits are described from the east to the west, whose breadth is to hold twenty-five thousand reeds, but the length as much as the individual tribes hold from the east to the sea; the number of this length is uncertain, for no measure was set down in the description of the individual tribes; but if the breadth has twenty-five thousand reeds, one may infer that the number of the length, which is always greater than the breadth, is much greater.
Commentary on Ezekiel

In the midst, moreover, the sanctuary is placed, beside the firstfruits which are set apart for the Lord, of a length of twenty-five thousand reeds and a breadth of ten thousand — reading which, we can say nothing else but that saying of the Apostle: O the depth of the riches and of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments, and untraceable his ways!, and in another place: That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, to know also the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God —. The number twenty-five, moreover, is referred to the senses — of which it was said: You shall possess a divine sense —, and that of ten thousand to perfect and consummate virtue — which by the decalogue of the old instrument reaches to the mystery of the Gospel; we touched on this briefly before, and here we shall recall it in part: for if, adding from one, you reach four, you will fill up the number ten, and so it will come about that the Old Testament is bound together in the New, and the New is expanded in the Old —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The sanctuary, moreover (that is, the temple) of the Lord, shall be in the midst of the priestly firstfruits, and it will be walled about on every part with equal sides; and because he had said: These moreover shall be the firstfruits of the sanctuary of the priests, lest under the common term all priests should claim for themselves the possession of this place and the ceremonies to be observed, he sets it down specifically, adding: The sanctuary shall be for the priests, of the sons of 'Sadoc' — which means 'righteous', of whom it is said: The Lord is righteous and has loved righteousnesses; his face has seen equity; for 'Sadoc' the Seventy write 'Saduc'. This Sadoc speaks in the Gospel: For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, and of him, under the name of Solomon, the prophet mystically sings: O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son —. Those priests, however, shall possess the sanctuary of the Lord and keep his ceremonies: Who did not go astray when the children of Israel and the Levites went astray, about whom there was discussion in the earlier parts: they do not offer victims but, content with the privilege of the name and with the humility of their error, always say in their heart: I know my iniquity, and my sin is ever against me — let the priestly rank hear this, and he who was overcome by the heat of the Arian persecution and afterwards bowed his neck to the true faith lest he lack wealth and power: let it be enough for him if he is not expelled from the temple, if he holds some shadow and image of his former name, and let him not, lolling back and belching up delicacies, as though spotless and pure, belch upon us from a most lofty throne the nausea of his ignorance and barbarous garrulity —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

These moreover shall be the firstfruits of the sanctuary of the priests: toward the north twenty-five thousand in length, and toward the sea ten thousand in breadth, and also toward the east ten thousand in breadth, and toward the south twenty-five thousand in length; and the sanctuary of the Lord shall be in the midst of it: the sanctuary for the priests, of the sons of Zadok, who kept my ceremonies and did not go astray when the children of Israel went astray, as the Levites went astray. And there shall be firstfruits from the firstfruits of the land, the Holy of Holies, beside the border of the Levites. The four sides of the firstfruits of the sanctuary are described — a portion which belongs not to the people or to the common crowd, nor to the Levites, a lower rank, but properly to the worship of the priests —: namely of the north and of the west and of the east and of the south; and part by part the order of progress is told: so that, leaving the cold of the north, we may come to the west, where, that is, our vices may set and perish, and thence pass over to the east, and, when the sun of righteousness has risen for us, come to the south, in which the light is brightest and perfect; and both from the north to the sea and from the east to the south there are to be twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth, so that everywhere the same measure of length and breadth may be kept.
Commentary on Ezekiel

For there shall be, he says, for 'them' firstfruits from the firstfruits of the land — that is, for the priests, and for those Who did not go astray when the children of Israel and the Levites went astray; and firstfruits from firstfruits, as tithes of tithes —, and the Holy of Holies beside the border of the Levites, so that the Levites indeed may have the borders adjoining the priests, but may not be able to hold the navel, that is, its middle, and the possession itself.
Commentary on Ezekiel

The possession of the Levites is also described, which is indeed neighboring to the borders of the priests, and has, for the multitude of the Levites, the same spaces in length and in breadth that the fewness of the priests has, but nevertheless uses its own boundaries and understands that it is separated from the priestly rank, to strike down the pride of the ministers who, ignorant of the humility of their station, swell up beyond the priests, that is, the presbyters: they reckon their dignity not by merit but by riches; certainly, whoever is first of the ministers, because he makes proclamation item by item among the people and yet does not depart from the side of the high priest, thinks it an injury if he is ordained a presbyter, and he does not remember, minister of tables and of widows, that he was appointed to the service not only of the priests but also of the widows and of the poor.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And also for the Levites likewise, beside the borders of the priests, twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth; the whole length twenty-five thousand and the breadth ten thousand; and they shall not sell of it, nor exchange (or measure), nor shall the firstfruits of the land be transferred (or taken away), because they are sanctified to the Lord. But the five thousand that remain in breadth by twenty-five thousand shall be profane, of the city, for dwelling and for suburbs; and the city shall be in the midst of it. What we have rendered as 'profane', for which Aquila translated βέβηλον, Symmachus and Theodotion λαικόν, the Seventy said προτείχισμα, which we can call 'outer wall'; but 'profane' and 'lay', that is, 'common', is what all the people may dwell in anywhere; and what they said: Nor shall it be measured nor taken away, for what we said: It shall not be exchanged nor transferred, plainly has no sense.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And they shall not sell, he says, of it, nor exchange, so that the possession of the Levitical allotment may remain eternal, and the merit of the dignity may not be overcome by price, nor be transferred from one to another: because the things that are sanctified to the Lord do not belong to those to whom they are given, but to him in whose name they are possessed.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But the five thousand that remain in breadth by twenty-five thousand — 'of length' is understood —, shall be profane, of the city, so that all the Israelites and anyone of the common people may dwell there; not that they are unclean, or that anything in the dwelling of the holy land is thought defiled and filthy, but that, besides the priests, all are permitted to dwell in them; by which we understand that all the things we refer to the senses, that is, to the desires of the body — what we take in by sight and hearing, by touch, smell and taste — are profane and do not have the sanctity of the temple, and are not of priestly privilege but of lay cheapness. And the city shall be in the midst — of which it is written: The rush of the river gladdens the city of God, and: A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden —; of it we shall speak in what follows. Προτείχισμα, that is, 'outer wall', and διάστημα, that is, 'space', which the Seventy translated for 'suburbs': what sense it has in this place we do not know.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And these the measures of the same: toward the northern side four thousand five hundred, and toward the southern side four thousand five hundred, and toward the eastern side four thousand five hundred, and toward the western side four thousand five hundred. As to his saying: And these are its measures, 'of the city' is to be understood; for at the end of the preceding chapter it was set down: And the city shall be in the midst of it, that is, of the land. And first he begins from the northern side and sets the southern side opposite it, and again he matches like with like, so as to set over against the eastern side the western, that is, the sea; and each side of the city has four thousand and five hundred reeds, which, when reckoned, make eleven thousand and eighty-five paces, so that the whole city together, as is written at the end of this volume, has eighteen thousand reeds round about, which make forty-four thousand paces and three hundred and forty — whence also Psalm 44 (45), which is entitled: To the end, for those who shall be changed, and pertains 'to Ididia', that is, 'to the beloved of the Lord', or, as Aquila translated, 'for the lilies', and Symmachus 'for the flowers', contains the mysteries of the Church, which is the city of the Lord, of which it is written in the same psalm: The queen stood at your right hand in gilded clothing, surrounded with variety, and again: All the glory of the king's daughter is within, so that she is not like tombs whitewashed outside, but washes all things of the dish both within and without —. And when we have withdrawn from the north, the coldest wind, we pass over to the south, and, after the light of knowledge has risen in us, we dread the setting of our strengths, considering by no means the things past but the things to come, and not holding a sure possession of virtue, but saying daily in prayer: Lead us not into temptation, which we cannot bear.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the suburbs of the city shall be toward the north two hundred fifty, and toward the south two hundred fifty, and toward the east two hundred fifty, and toward the sea two hundred fifty. For 'suburbs', which in Hebrew are called 'magras', the Seventy again translated διάστημα, that is, 'space'. As to its saying 'two hundred fifty' on each side, 'reeds' is understood, which have six cubits each and one handbreadth, and on each side they make a little less than six hundred and seventeen paces, and all together a thousand reeds, amounting to two thousand four hundred and sixty-eight paces: these spaces surround the walls of the city round about, so as to divide between the city and the things that remain. From this it is shown that no one, whether of those who carry out the works of the city or of those gathering produce, has license over these spaces, but that they are free from the use and work of men, so that the surroundings of the city walls may have the pleasantness of shrubs and herbs springing up of their own accord, and of the other things that the earth brings forth.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And what remains in length alongside the firstfruits of the sanctuary, ten thousand to the east and ten thousand to the west, shall be as the firstfruits of the sanctuary, and its produce shall be for food (or for loaves) for those who serve (or work) in the works of the city. And those serving (or working) in the works of the city shall serve the city (or shall work) from all the tribes of Israel. All the firstfruits of twenty-five thousand, by twenty-five thousand foursquare, shall be set apart for the firstfruits of the sanctuary and the possession of the city. After the description of the holy city and its suburbs, he wishes the remaining part of the firstfruits of the sanctuary, ten thousand reeds stretching to the east and another ten thousand to the west, to be assigned to those who carry out the works of the city for various uses and for whatever the city needs: namely, that they be sown, and that the workers feed on the produce that grows in this space of land, those who either build the walls of the city or restore what is broken and ruinous, so that the city may have its adornment, and its roofs be kept in repair and restored when necessity demands — and this we find done not only in Israel or in the possession of the holy land, which spiritually contain the mysteries of the Church, but in the Roman empire too, so that certain estates belong to the jurisdiction of cities, either by royal munificence or by the inheritances and donation of many, lest, namely, the buildings gradually collapse and the public edifices, which are an ornament to the city, be harmed by long neglect —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And the workers, he says (or those who serve in the works of the city), shall be from all the tribes of Israel, so that no one may think himself exempt from the works of the city, but all may vie with one another in building up the Church — which we read was done in the tabernacle too, so that, according to the variety of their means, one offered gold and silver, scarlet, fine linen and purple, and various and diverse woofs, others skins and goats' hair; and, though the gifts were diverse according to the measure of their substance, the reward of the givers was one, nay rather greater for those who offered small things indeed but greater in proportion to their means, after the example of the poor widow who put two mites into the gifts of the treasury and was praised by the judgment of the Lord, who said: Truly I say to you that this poor little widow has put in more than all; for all these out of their abundance have put into the gifts of God, but she out of that which she lacks has put in all the living that she had —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

As therefore we have spoken about the works of the city, so this must be touched on briefly: that all the firstfruits of the sanctuary and the possession of the city, reckoned together foursquare, contain two hundred and forty-six thousand and a third part — for if twenty-five thousand reeds — which have six cubits each and one handbreadth — make of our paces, that is, Roman paces, sixty-one thousand six hundred and sixty-seven, no one doubts that these, reckoned fourfold, produce the number above —; from which we perceive that all things are to be understood spiritually, and that the possession of the Church is much broader than it once was in Judea, where they did not even receive portions of the holy land, but from the individual tribes received, in forty-eight cities, not a full possession but a dwelling and lodgings; so that those too who seem to be lay and not to have attained to the priestly and Levitical rank may nevertheless, if they work for the city of the Lord, feed on the holy land of the meek, and on the land of believers, one of whom said: I believe I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And what remains shall be the prince's, on every side (or on this side and that) of the firstfruits of the sanctuary and of the possession of the city, over against (or before the face of) the twenty-five thousand of the firstfruits as far as the eastern border, and also from the sea over against (or before the face of) the twenty-five thousand as far as the border of the sea, likewise in the portions of the prince it shall be; and the firstfruits of the sanctuary and the sanctuary of the temple shall be in the midst of it. And of the possession of the Levites and of the possession of the city, in the midst of the portions of the prince, it shall be toward the border of Judah and toward the border of Benjamin, and shall belong to the prince. About this prince it was argued more fully above, and that he alone was to receive as much as one tribe; but now we learn something else: that whatever remains from all the tribes, he alone receives, so that there is no tribe that does not offer gifts to the prince, not from elsewhere but from the firstfruits which serve the temple and the sanctuary and the parts assigned to the city — for this is what he says: Over against (or before the face of) the twenty-five thousand of the firstfruits as far as the eastern border (or as far as the eastern border of the sea), so that the firstfruits are between the seven and the five, and in the firstfruits themselves the city and its suburbs, and in the midst of the city the sanctuary of the temple —.
Commentary on Ezekiel

But also whatever remains of the possession of the Levites and of the possession of the city will be allotted to the prince, and the furthest part of the seven tribes, neighboring the firstfruits and the city and the temple, will be in the tribe of Judah, and the furthest part of the five tribes, by the same right as above, in the tribe of Benjamin; and that furthest part itself will belong to the prince. Hence the mysteries of holy Scripture are to be marveled at, and pondered rather than set forth in speech. For in the earlier division of the lands beyond the Jordan, through Moses, the land was divided to the two tribes, Reuben and Gad, and to the half tribe of Manasseh; but within the Jordan, through Joshua son of Nun and Eleazar son of Aaron, Judah took possession on the south, and Ephraim and the half tribe of Manasseh on the north; afterwards, however, when spies had been sent out from Shiloh through the individual tribes and the description of the land had been brought to Joshua and Eleazar, Benjamin received a possession beside Judah on the south and beside Ephraim and the half tribe of Manasseh; the second tribe, Simeon, received its inheritance within the tribe of Judah — that what is written of Levi and Simeon might be fulfilled: I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel —; the third, Zebulun, received Galilee, in which is Mount Tabor; the fourth, Issachar, where Jezreel is, as far as the Jordan; the fifth, Asher, as far as Mount Carmel, which overhangs the Great Sea, and Tyre and Sidon; the sixth, Naphtali, in Galilee as far as the Jordan, where Tiberias is, which was once called Chinnereth; the seventh, Dan, as far as Joppa, where are the cities of Aijalon and Selebi and Emmaus, which is now called Nicopolis — although we have read that afterwards, passing over other tribes, they took for themselves the city of Leshem in the tribe of Dan, which today is called Paneas. Since these things are so, and there is so great a difference between the earlier description of the tribes and the one now given, let us consider this: how, both in the present description and in the past one, the city and the temple are placed between the tribe of Judah and Benjamin; and in the earlier description Judah was on the south and Benjamin on the north, but here, on the contrary, it comes about that Judah is on the north and Benjamin on the south; after whom the second is Simeon, the third Issachar, the fourth Zebulun, the fifth Gad: namely five tribes, as is said in what follows; for it is written:
Commentary on Ezekiel

And for the remaining tribes: from the eastern side to the western side, Benjamin one. And over against the border of Benjamin, from the eastern side to the western side, Simeon one. And above the border of Simeon, from the eastern side to the side of the west, Issachar one. And above the border of Issachar, from the eastern side to the western side, Zebulun one. And above the border of Zebulun, from the eastern side to the side of the sea, Gad one. And above the border of Gad, toward the side of the south, toward the midday; and the boundary shall be from Tamar as far as the waters of Contradiction, Kadesh, and the inheritance over against the Great Sea. This is the land which you shall allot to the children of Israel, and these are their divisions, says the Lord God. As to the fact that with the five and the seven tribes 'una' [one, in the feminine] is always placed at the end, either 'part' or 'possession' or 'inheritance' is understood, although Aquila and Symmachus translate in the neuter gender τό ὅριον, which signifies 'border'.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And this is briefly to be noted: that the tribe of Gad, the last of the five tribes — which in the earlier description was beyond the Jordan — is placed in that part which Judah held before, namely toward the side of the south, toward the midday, and that the boundary is from Thamar as far as the waters of Contradiction, Kadesh, the inheritance over against the Great Sea; Thamar is the very place of which we have already spoken, which they now call 'Palmyra', and which was once built by Solomon: for 'palm' in the Hebrew tongue is called 'Thamar', and some think it obtained this name from the fact that there are very many palm groves there. And as to what follows: As far as the waters of Contradiction, Kadesh, the inheritance over against the Great Sea (for which the Seventy translated from Theman and the water of Mariboth, Kadesh, the inheritance as far as the Great Sea), this is to be observed: that in the Hebrew the same word 'nehela', because it is ambiguous, means both 'inheritance' and 'torrent', and that here it ought to be taken as 'torrent' rather than 'inheritance': for this is the torrent which enters the Great Sea at Rhinocorura, as we have already said before; Kadesh, moreover, which in the book of Joshua is called Cadesbarne, is in the desert which extends as far as the city of Petra; 'Mariboth', however, which means 'of Contradiction', is not the name of a place, as most suppose, but of the waters at which the people contradicted the Lord and Moses offended God, as the psalm says: They tempted him at the water of Contradiction, and Moses was afflicted on their account. And the whole inheritance of the holy land on the southern side, beside the borders of Egypt, is bounded by the torrent of Rhinocorura. And because 'Gad' means 'temptation', in his possession we pass from the palm groves to the waters of Contradiction, as far as 'Cades', which means 'holy', so that we may understand that even after the victory over the world we ought to be anxious and always in fear, and to remember that little verse: The life of men upon earth is temptation, and to arrive at holiness while adversaries resist, and so to obtain the victory; and let us contemplate close at hand the torrent full of rains.
Against Marcion, Book III, Chapter 25

But we do confess that a kingdom is promised to us upon the earth, although before heaven, only in another state of existence; inasmuch as it will be after the resurrection for a thousand years in the divinely-built city of Jerusalem, "let down from heaven," [Revelation 21:2] which the apostle also calls "our mother from above;" [Galatians 4:26] and, while declaring that our πολίτευμα, or citizenship, is in heaven, he predicates of it that it is really a city in heaven. This both Ezekiel had knowledge of [Ezekiel 48:30-35] and the Apostle John beheld. [Revelation 21:10-23] And the word of the new prophecy which is a part of our belief, attests how it foretold that there would be for a sign a picture of this very city exhibited to view previous to its manifestation. This prophecy, indeed, has been very lately fulfilled in an expedition to the East. For it is evident from the testimony of even heathen witnesses, that in Judæa there was suspended in the sky a city early every morning for forty days. As the day advanced, the entire figure of its walls would wane gradually, and sometimes it would vanish instantly. We say that this city has been provided by God for receiving the saints on their resurrection, and refreshing them with the abundance of all really spiritual blessings, as a recompense for those which in the world we have either despised or lost; since it is both just and God-worthy that His servants should have their joy in the place where they have also suffered affliction for His name's sake. Of the heavenly kingdom this is the process. After its thousand years are over, within which period is completed the resurrection of the saints, who rise sooner or later according to their deserts there will ensue the destruction of the world and the conflagration of all things at the judgment: we shall then be changed in a moment into the substance of angels, even by the investiture of an incorruptible nature, and so be removed to that kingdom in heaven of which we have now been treating, just as if it had not been predicted by the Creator, and as if it were proving Christ to belong to the other god and as if he were the first and sole revealer of it.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And these are the outgoings of the city: from the northern side you shall measure four thousand five hundred. And the gates of the city after the names of the tribes of Israel: three gates from the north, the gate of Reuben one, the gate of Judah one, the gate of Levi one. And toward the eastern side four thousand five hundred; and three gates: the gate of Joseph one, the gate of Benjamin one, the gate of Dan one. And toward the southern side you shall measure four thousand five hundred: the gate of Simeon one, the gate of Issachar one, the gate of Zebulun one. And toward the western side four thousand five hundred; their gates three: the gate of Gad one, the gate of Asher one, the gate of Naphtali one. Round about eighteen thousand; and the name of the city from that day: The Lord is there. Concerning the circuit of the city, that on each side, foursquare, it had four thousand five hundred reeds, the preceding discourse has told; these make eighteen thousand reeds, as is also set down in the present chapter, that is, forty-four thousand paces and three hundred and forty paces. Now it is written that on each side, that is, along eleven thousand paces and eighty-five paces, there were three gates, which Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion call διεξόδους, the Seventy διεκβολάς, and which we have translated 'outgoings' and 'exits' of the city. And first this is to be briefly pointed out: that the same tribes encamped around the tabernacle in such a way that on the east were Judah, Issachar and Zebulun, sons of Leah; and on the south Reuben, Simeon, Gad, two sons of Leah and the third a son of Zilpah, Leah's handmaid; but on the west Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin, namely two sons of Rachel — because Joseph, in place of the tribe of Levi, which was assigned to the sacrifices, was divided into two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh —; and on the north Dan and Asher and Naphtali, of whom the first and the third are sons of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid, the second a son of Zilpah, Leah's handmaid: ignoble, and placed toward the north, inasmuch as they were begotten of the stock of handmaids at odds with one another. This is according to the book of Numbers and the description of the tabernacle which, at God's command, was dictated by the mouth of Moses. But our city — which is The city of the great king: Whose artificer and founder is God, of which the psalmist also sings: Will Zion say: A man, and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her? — has another description of the tribes in the holy land, and another measure of the city, order of possession and sides of the individual tribes. For first, three gates or exits of the city are set over against the northern side, of which are Reuben the firstborn, and Judah, the founder of the royal stock, and Levi, about whose name nothing was said in the description of the tabernacle and of the camp: so that, possessing the birthright, as a royal and priestly race, we may despise the cold of the north; secondly, toward the east are Joseph, Benjamin and Dan, both sons of Rachel and one of Bilhah her handmaid; toward the south, Simeon, Issachar and Zebulun, of whom three are sons of Leah; further, toward the west Gad, Asher and Naphtali, of whom the first two are sons of Zilpah, Leah's handmaid, the third a son of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid — Who is wise, and will understand these things? understanding, will know them? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous will walk in them; but the transgressors will fall in them —. These twelve gates or exits, I think, were joined to the individual tribes, according to the quality of their merits and virtues, under the names of the apostles and of the patriarchs; of them it is written more openly in the Revelation of John too, and the wonderful mysteries of the divine Scriptures bear witness.
Commentary on Ezekiel

And it is necessary that such a city hold eighteen thousand reeds round about, under which number, in Psalm 18 (19) also, the natural law is set down, and the grace of the Gospel is described, by which the Church, that is, the city of the Savior, has been built. The name of the city itself, too, will by no means be, as before, 'Hierosolyma', which means 'vision of peace', but 'Adonai sam', which is rendered into the Latin tongue 'The Lord is there': who will never withdraw from her, as he departed before from the former people, saying to the disciples: Arise, let us go hence, and to the Jews: Your house shall be left to you desolate, but will have an eternal possession and himself be her possession, promising to the same disciples: Behold, I am with you even to the consummation of the age.
